title: Hypothesis Testing Assignment
text:
This assignment follows the DP as Hypothesis Testing blog post. Complete the exercises below using only imports from libdpy.
Code
from scipy.stats import norm

from libdpy.hypothesis_testing import (
    FPR_from_threshold,
    TPR_from_threshold,
    threshold_from_FPR,
)
from libdpy.visualization.privacy_plots import PrivacyPlot

title: Hypothesis Testing Assignment
text:
Exercise 1 — Thresholds and error rates
Consider distinguishing \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) (negative) from \(\mathcal{N}(1, 1)\) (positive) with the decision rule “classify values above a threshold as positive.”

Choose a threshold that yields false positive rate \(0.05\).
Report the corresponding true positive rate.
Verify your answers with FPR_from_threshold and TPR_from_threshold.



Code
dist_neg = norm(0, 1)
dist_pos = norm(1, 1)

target_fpr = 0.05
threshold = threshold_from_FPR(dist_neg, target_fpr)
tpr = TPR_from_threshold(dist_pos, threshold)

print(f"threshold = {threshold:.4f}")
print(f"TPR = {tpr:.4f}")
print(f"FPR check = {FPR_from_threshold(dist_neg, threshold):.4f}")


threshold = 1.6449
TPR = 0.2595
FPR check = 0.0500

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
text:
Our “true data” in this lecture
Fulton is public, so we can inspect these examples. From now on, however, treat the fixed discretized construction partition as the confidential ground-truth table \(D_{\mathrm{true}}\). Every synthetic release may depend on \(D_{\mathrm{true}}\) only through its explicitly accounted private measurements.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
text:
Public contract

Private: the fixed Fulton construction partition.
Public: eight categorical domains with \(D=29{,}568\), including seven named 2000 Fulton PUMA areas and eleven ordered person-income brackets.
Adjacency: substitute one row; every release uses \((\varepsilon,\delta)=(1,10^{-5})\).
Accounting: compose Gaussian measurements in \(\rho\)-zCDP.
Through-statistic: education \(\rightarrow\) the ordered income distribution.

Adjacency is part of the guarantee, not a footnote. This lecture substitutes one row: a neighbouring table has the same \(n\) with one person replaced. Lecture 12 adds or removes one row instead, so its \(n\) changes by one. The two conventions are not interchangeable, and an \(\varepsilon=1\) substitution guarantee is in general the stronger claim, because one substitution is one removal followed by one addition. When we compare a Lecture 11 number with a Lecture 12 number, we are comparing mechanisms under two different neighbour relations, not two points on one scale.
The last variable is total person income (PUMS PINCP), not salary: it can be zero or negative. We use one Nonpositive income category rather than spend a separate cell on losses and another on zero, followed by \(\$1\)–\(9{,}999\) and the public dollar cut points above \(\$10{,}000\). This gives eleven useful, ordered categories while retaining the \(\$50{,}000\) boundary used later.
If analysts only need a fixed query workload, releasing those answers directly is usually simpler and more accurate than manufacturing general-purpose rows.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
text:
A real-world example: IOM / CTDC
This is the one case for which the primary sources support the complete story needed here: an actual downloadable release, a formal differential-privacy claim, a documented construction mechanism, and a source-produced visual.

What was released
The official CTDC release page provides a downloadable synthetic CSV, codebook, and data dictionary. CTDC says the release represents case data from more than 17,000 victims and survivors identified in 123 countries and territories, together with their accounts of more than 37,000 perpetrators, covering 2005–2022. The codebook describes 16 released variables: seven about victims, citizenship, and exploitation and nine about victims’ accounts of perpetrators.
The same CTDC page and the Microsoft Research release note state that this release provides differential privacy. Neither linked source states a numerical \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) value, so none is asserted here.


The released synthetic product, shown by CTDC



CTDC Global Victim–Perpetrator Synthetic Data dashboard, with victim and perpetrator characteristic summaries.


Source-produced dashboard screenshot, not a course reconstruction and not confidential microdata. The dashboard accompanies the official CTDC synthetic-data release. Credit: “Source: Counter-Trafficking Data Collaborative (CTDC), July 2026.”


How the sources describe the mechanism
Microsoft’s official algorithm documentation and the codebook describe the same two stages:

query counts of short combinations of case attributes and release those counts with differential privacy; then
sample synthetic records from the private aggregate counts.

The second stage is post-processing, so the synthetic records retain the privacy guarantee of the aggregate counts. The codebook also warns that these are reported cases, not a random sample of trafficking victims worldwide, and therefore should not be used to estimate prevalence.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
section: Start with a Gaussian whose mean is unknown
text:
Start with a Gaussian whose mean is unknown
Suppose the private observations follow a Gaussian model with unknown mean \(\mu\) and known standard deviation \(\sigma\):
\[
X_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2).
\]
The experiment fixes \(n=2{,}000\), \(\mu=0\), known \(\sigma=1\), public clipping bounds \([L,U]=[-6,6]\), and \((\varepsilon,\delta)=(1,10^{-6})\), which converts to \(\rho\approx0.01747\). It releases \(m=n=2{,}000\) synthetic rows and uses 12,000 repeated experiments (3,000 in notebook smoke tests). For a standard Gaussian, \(\Pr(|X-\mu|>6\sigma)\approx2\times10^{-9}\); by a union bound, the probability that any of the 2,000 observations is clipped is below \(4\times10^{-6}\). Thus the no-clipping approximation used below holds with high probability under the stated model.
An unbounded Gaussian sample mean has infinite global sensitivity. We therefore declare public bounds \([L,U]\) and clip each observation before computing \(\overline X\). Under substitution adjacency,
\[
\Delta_2\overline X=\frac{U-L}{n}.
\]
The Gaussian mechanism releases the fitted mean
\[
\widetilde\mu=\Pi_{[L,U]}(\overline X+Z),\qquad
Z\sim\mathcal N(0,s_{\mathrm{DP}}^2),\qquad
s_{\mathrm{DP}}=\frac{U-L}{n\sqrt{2\rho}}.
\]
When clipping and projection are rare,
\[
\widetilde\mu\approx
\mathcal N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+s_{\mathrm{DP}}^2\right).
\]
Thus the private estimate looks like an ordinary Gaussian sample mean with slightly more variance—or an effective sample size \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sigma^2/(\sigma^2/n+s_{\mathrm{DP}}^2)\) smaller than \(n\).
Now draw \(Y_j^*\sim\mathcal N(\widetilde\mu,\sigma^2)\) and release \(Y_j=\Pi_{[L,U]}(Y_j^*)\) for \(j=1,\ldots,n\). When clipping is rare, their mean adds one more sampling term:
\[
\overline Y\approx
\mathcal N\!\left(
\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+s_{\mathrm{DP}}^2+\frac{\sigma^2}{n}
\right).
\]
Sampling the synthetic rows is randomized postprocessing, so it cannot weaken the Gaussian mechanism’s guarantee. We postpone the separate question—whether sampling alone can provide privacy—until after seeing the Binomial analogue.
The next experiment runs the actual clipped mechanism repeatedly rather than drawing the displayed curves from the no-clipping approximation. Its legend reports the original construction size as exact \(n=2{,}000\); its derived \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\) labels use the analytic no-clipping variances.


Code
gaussian_example = build_gaussian_parametric_example(
    epsilon=PARAMETRIC_EPSILON,
    delta=PARAMETRIC_DELTA,
    smoke=SMOKE,
)
show_figure(parametric_pdf_cdf_figure(gaussian_example))









Both panels show the same three Gaussian estimators. The left panel is a smoothed empirical density; the right is the empirical CDF. The DP fitted mean is slightly wider than the ordinary sample mean, and the mean of the released rows is wider again. The synthetic rows are useful output, but they are not \(n\) new observations from the original population. Standard errors computed as if they were fresh evidence therefore answer the wrong question.
Why might a Monte-Carlo estimate previously have shown the original \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\) as close to, but not exactly, 2,000? It estimated variance from finitely many repeated, clipped samples. Finite simulation error and the very rare clipping events perturb that estimate. Analytically, \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline X)=\sigma^2/n\), hence \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sigma^2/(\sigma^2/n)=n\) under the displayed no-clipping Gaussian model. The figure now reports that analytic value.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
text:
Second step: the Binomial model
Now let \(S\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\) be the number of successes and \(\widehat p=S/n\) the sample mean. Its substitution sensitivity is \(1/n\). Apply the same two-step construction:
Here the chosen values are \(n=2{,}000\), \(p=0.35\), \((\varepsilon,\delta)=(1,10^{-6})\), hence \(\rho\approx0.01747\), and \(m=n=2{,}000\) released Bernoulli rows. The experiment uses 60,000 repetitions (20,000 in notebook smoke tests).
\[
\widetilde p=\Pi_{[0,1]}(\widehat p+Z),\qquad
Z\sim\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{1}{2\rho n^2}\right),
\]
\[
T\mid\widetilde p\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\widetilde p),
\qquad \overline Y=T/n.
\]
Ignoring the rare projection at 0 or 1, match the variance of \(\overline Y\) to \(p(1-p)/n_{\mathrm{eff}}\). This predicts an ordinary Binomial experiment with a smaller effective sample size. We use the same plot as for the Gaussian: a density/mass view on the left and an empirical CDF on the right. The ordinary effective-size Binomial reference appears in both panels.


Code
binomial_example = build_binomial_parametric_example(
    epsilon=PARAMETRIC_EPSILON,
    delta=PARAMETRIC_DELTA,
    smoke=SMOKE,
)
show_figure(parametric_pdf_cdf_figure(binomial_example))









The density/mass and CDF views tell the same story: the released-row curve nearly coincides with the ordinary Binomial reference at the displayed \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\). Again, generating \(n\) rows did not create \(n\) fresh observations; it produced a noisier estimate whose uncertainty is well described by a smaller effective sample.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
text:
Privacy from resampling alone
Now remove the separately added Gaussian noise and ask how many synthetic rows sampling itself can release. The answer is model-dependent.
Gaussian rows. Release \(m\) independent rows from \(\mathcal N(\overline X,\sigma^2)\) after clipping the original observations to the same public \([L,U]=[-6,6]\). With \(\Delta=(U-L)/n\), the complete output is
\[
\rho_G(m)=\frac{m\Delta^2}{2\sigma^2}\text{-zCDP},\qquad
\varepsilon_G(m,\delta)=\rho_G(m)+2\sqrt{\rho_G(m)\log(1/\delta)}.
\]
Bernoulli rows. Truncate the empirical probability to the public interval \([a,1-a]=[0.1,0.9]\). For neighboring datasets, call the two truncated values \(p\) and \(q\). Projection is nonexpansive, so \(|p-q|\leq1/n\) everywhere on that interval. If the released sample contains \(K\) ones, then under \(K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,p)\) its privacy loss against \(q\) is
\[
L_{p,q}(K)
=m\,\operatorname{KL}(\operatorname{Ber}(p)\|\operatorname{Ber}(q))
+(K-mp)\bigl(\operatorname{logit}(p)-\operatorname{logit}(q)\bigr).
\]
Over the entire truncated range,
\[
\operatorname{KL}(\operatorname{Ber}(p)\|\operatorname{Ber}(q))
\leq\frac{1}{n^2a(1-a)},\qquad
|\operatorname{logit}(p)-\operatorname{logit}(q)|
\leq\frac{1}{na(1-a)}.
\]
Hoeffding’s inequality therefore gives, in both neighboring directions,
\[
\Pr\!\left[L_{p,q}>
\frac{m}{n^2a(1-a)}
+\frac{1}{na(1-a)}\sqrt{\frac{m}{2}\log\frac1\delta}
\right]\leq\delta.
\]
Thus the entire \(m\)-row Bernoulli release, not a per-bit composition, is \((\varepsilon_B(m,\delta),\delta)\)-DP with
\[
\varepsilon_B(m,\delta)=
\frac{m}{n^2a(1-a)}
+\frac{1}{na(1-a)}\sqrt{\frac{m}{2}\log\frac1\delta}.
\]
The plot uses \(m/n\) on the horizontal axis, so the vertical line at \(m/n=1\) always means “release as many rows as were in the original sample.” The title now holds the original sample size fixed at \(n=2{,}000\) for both mechanisms. The vertical axis is simply \(\varepsilon\); both curves use \(\delta=10^{-6}\). Both guarantees grow at the same leading \(\sqrt m/n\) rate. Their remaining quantitative difference comes from the public model constants shown in the title: Gaussian width \(12\sigma\) versus the Bernoulli interval \([0.1,0.9]\).
The Bernoulli truncation is essential: if probabilities may reach 0 or 1, a neighboring input can give an output positive probability versus zero probability, so no finite likelihood-ratio bound follows.


Code
resampling_tradeoff = build_resampling_privacy_tradeoff(
    epsilon=PARAMETRIC_EPSILON,
    delta=PARAMETRIC_DELTA,
)
show_figure(resampling_privacy_tradeoff_figure(resampling_tradeoff))

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
text:
Extend beyond parametric families
The Gaussian and Binomial examples each estimated one unknown parameter. Our Fulton table has eight categorical columns, and a complete row can occupy
\[
D=2\times6\times4\times2\times2\times2\times7\times11
=29{,}568
\]
joint cells. An unrestricted joint distribution therefore has 29,567 free probabilities. Estimating that complete object is possible, but it spends noise on many combinations that may be rare or irrelevant.
We instead begin with smaller tables. A one-way table asks only how often each category appears in one column. A two-way table asks how often two categories appear together. After privately measuring selected tables, we fit one valid 29,568-cell distribution consistent with them as closely as possible and sample complete rows from that fit.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
section: Temptation: make every column look right
text:
Temptation: make every column look right
For column \(j\) with \(d_j\) categories, release the complete normalized histogram
\[
q_j(D)=\left(\frac1n\sum_i\mathbf1\{x_{ij}=a\}\right)_{a=1}^{d_j}.
\]
Replacing one row can remove mass \(1/n\) from one category and add it to another, so the whole vector has \(L_2\) sensitivity \(\sqrt2/n\). The eight column histograms contain
\[
2+6+4+2+2+2+7+11=36
\]
cells in total, but they are eight vector queries—not 36 separately composed scalar queries.
Where does the 8 come from? There are exactly eight released column vectors: sex, age, education, employment, marriage, minor children, PUMA, and income. Convert the common \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) target to total \(\rho\) and assign \(\rho_j=\rho/8\) to each of those eight vectors. For every coordinate of vector \(j\), add independent noise
\[
\mathcal N(0,\sigma_j^2),\qquad
\sigma_j=\frac{\sqrt2/n}{\sqrt{2\rho_j}}
=\frac1{n\sqrt{\rho_j}}.
\]
zCDP composition adds the eight vector costs:
\[
\sum_{j=1}^8\rho_j=8\left(\frac\rho8\right)=\rho.
\]
For the full notebook run, \(n=20{,}613\) and \(\rho=0.02081994\), so each vector gets \(\rho_j=0.00260249\), \(\Delta_2=\sqrt2/n=0.00006861\), and every coordinate receives Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(0.00095096\). Within a vector, the \(d_j\) noisy coordinates are already covered by that vector’s sensitivity calculation; we do not compose again over categories.
Project each noisy vector to its probability simplex and sample the columns independently:
\[
\widehat p_{\mathrm{1way}}(x)
=\prod_{j=1}^8\widehat q_j(x_j).
\]
This construction is designed to make every column look right. Education uses four of the 36 released cells and person income uses eleven. After introducing two-way measurement, we will compare these direct noisy one-ways with the one-way marginals induced by one noisy education × income table.


Code
show_figure(one_way_marginals_figure(
    artifact.diagnostics["one_way_marginal_comparison"],
    income_labels=artifact.contract.income_bin_labels,
    theory_sd=artifact.diagnostics["one_way_marginal_theory_sd"],
    methods=("truth", "one-way noisy"),
))










Downside: one-way marginals do not determine relationships
The left panel is the actual Fulton education × income joint used as the truth reference in this notebook. Its true income marginal sits immediately above it, and its true education marginal sits immediately to its right.
The right panel is a public mathematical illustration of independence: \(A_{ei}=p_E(e)p_I(i)\). It is not the private one-way release, not sampled synthetic data, and not a fit to Fulton. Its fixed illustrative education and income marginals are shown around the table so the independence construction is fully specified. Its role is only to show how multiplying one-way probabilities fills a \(4\times11\) joint table. The next figure performs the actual comparison against the exact and private one-way products used by the lecture artifact.


Code
show_figure(one_way_correlation_heatmap_figure(
    artifact.diagnostics["reference_education_income_joint"],
    correlation_diagnostic.product_joint,
    correlation_diagnostic.education_marginal,
    correlation_diagnostic.income_marginal,
    education_labels=(
        "below HS",
        "HS / some college",
        "associate / BA",
        "graduate / professional",
    ),
    income_labels=artifact.contract.income_bin_labels,
))









The one-way fit does what it promised: each education and income marginal is close. But those 4 and 11 cells do not determine the \(4\times11=44\) cells in the education × income table.
The next figure follows six fixed, interpretable cells through four stages:

their frequency in the real joint table;
the product of the exact, nonprivate one-way marginals;
the product of the private one-way marginals; and
their frequency after sampling the released synthetic rows.

The first gap is independence misspecification, the second is DP measurement error, and the third is finite synthetic-sample variation.


Code
show_figure(one_way_pair_cells_figure(
    artifact.reference,
    artifact.distributions["exact product"],
    artifact.distributions["one-way"],
    artifact.releases["one-way"],
    income_labels=artifact.contract.income_bin_labels,
))

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
text:
Measure complete two-way tables
To preserve relationships, measure joint categories rather than multiplying separate one-way probabilities. For columns \(j\) and \(k\) with \(d_jd_k\) joint cells, define the complete normalized contingency-table vector
\[
q_{jk}(D)=\left(
\frac1n\sum_i\mathbf1\{x_{ij}=a,x_{ik}=b\}
\right)_{(a,b)}\in\mathbb R^{d_jd_k}.
\]
A substituted row again moves mass \(1/n\) from at most one joint cell to another, so the whole pair vector has \(L_2\) sensitivity \(\sqrt2/n\), regardless of whether it contains 4 cells, 44 cells, or another pair-specific count.
For one pair allocated \(\rho_{jk}\), the private mechanism is
\[
\widetilde q_{jk}=q_{jk}(D)
+\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{jk}^2I_{d_jd_k}),\qquad
\sigma_{jk}=\frac{\sqrt2/n}{\sqrt{2\rho_{jk}}}
=\frac1{n\sqrt{\rho_{jk}}}.
\]
There are \(\binom82=28\) column pairs containing \(\sum_{j<k}d_jd_k=529\) pair cells. The all-pairs alternative is one fresh release: allocate \(\rho_{jk}=\rho/28\) to each of the 28 complete vectors, add independent Gaussian noise to all 529 coordinates, and compose \(\sum_{j<k}\rho_{jk}=\rho\). Privacy composition is over 28 vector mechanisms, not over 529 scalar cells.
The 28 noisy tables overlap and generally disagree. Rather than project each one independently, retain every raw vector \(y_r\), its marginalization operator \(A_r\), and its Gaussian scale \(\sigma_r\), then fit one joint distribution:
\[
\widehat p=\arg\min_{p\in\Delta_D}
\sum_r\frac{\|A_rp-y_r\|_2^2}{2\sigma_r^2}-\tau H(p).
\]
The next figure isolates one of those 28 already-accounted-for tables. It shows the education × income slice: the real \(4\times11\) table, its raw private measurement from the all-pairs release, and the same measurement after replacing negative cells by zero and renormalizing. The plot does not represent a single-pair mechanism; all 28 tables were measured at \(\rho/28\) before this one was selected for display. It uses the same blue heatmap-plus-marginals grammar as the earlier fixed-marginal diagnostic.


Code
show_figure(two_way_measurement_figure(
    artifact.diagnostics["two_way_table_comparison"],
    education_labels=(
        "below HS",
        "HS / some college",
        "associate / BA",
        "graduate / professional",
    ),
    income_labels=artifact.contract.income_bin_labels,
))










Downside: two-way tables give noisier one-way answers
All pairs preserve much more dependence, but divide the fixed privacy budget across 28 tables whether or not the analyst needs them. A pair vector does not have greater \(L_2\) sensitivity than a one-way vector: both have \(\sqrt2/n\). The loss begins with budget fragmentation: \(\rho/28\) per pair rather than \(\rho/8\) per one-way vector makes each pair-cell noise standard deviation \(\sqrt{28/8}\approx1.87\) times larger.
Marginalizing then sums independent noisy cells. The education marginal sums eleven income cells, so its expected noise standard deviation is \(\sqrt{11}\sqrt{28/8}\approx6.20\) times the direct one-way value. The income marginal sums four education cells, giving a factor \(\sqrt4\sqrt{28/8}\approx3.74\). The next figure compares those induced marginals with the dedicated one-way measurements. The raw result is shown before validity postprocessing so truncation cannot hide the accumulated measurement noise.


Code
show_figure(one_way_marginals_figure(
    artifact.diagnostics["one_way_marginal_comparison"],
    income_labels=artifact.contract.income_bin_labels,
    theory_sd=artifact.diagnostics["one_way_marginal_theory_sd"],
))









The black bars are the real-data truth. The direct one-way release is usually closest because each vector receives \(\rho/8\). The raw two-way table receives only \(\rho/28\) and can induce negative marginal cells. Truncation restores a valid table, but it is postprocessing rather than recovered information: it can move every marginal when it removes negative joint cells and renormalizes.
That bar plot follows the education × income table alone, but the all-pairs release contains seven independently noised pair tables involving education and seven involving income. Marginalizing each overlapping table therefore gives seven different answers to the same one-way question. The next heatmaps show those raw pair-induced answers minus truth. A noise-aware joint fit restores formal consistency by finding one compromise distribution; it cannot make the inconsistent measurements simultaneously exact or recover the noise-free answer.


Code
show_figure(two_way_inconsistency_figure(
    artifact.diagnostics["pairwise_one_way_inconsistency"],
    education_labels=(
        "below HS",
        "HS / some college",
        "associate / BA",
        "graduate / professional",
    ),
    income_labels=artifact.contract.income_bin_labels,
))

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
text:
Three-way relationships remain unidentified
Now use three binary variables because they have exactly eight inspectable states. The top row of the next figure first shows everything a one- and two-way release can learn: every binary one-way is 50/50 and every pair is uniform over 00, 01, 10, and 11. The bottom row then reveals two possible three-way truths. Even parity and odd parity put mass on opposite sets of four states while matching every displayed one- and two-way marginal perfectly. Thus all 28 Fulton pairs can improve pairwise accuracy without identifying a three-way relationship.


Code
parity_state = artifact.diagnostics["parity"]
show_figure(parity_witness_figure(
    parity_state["even"],
    parity_state["odd"],
))

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
text:
Temptation: add every three-way marginal
The parity witness suggests measuring triples next. With eight columns, however, Fulton has \(\binom83=56\) three-way vectors containing 4,154 cells. Under the same total budget, each vector would receive only \(\rho/56\)—and four-way relationships would still remain unidentified. Repeating “measure every order” eventually becomes the 29,568-cell full joint.
Repeating this strategy measures a growing collection of statistics without ever making the resulting table universally accurate. We now test that limitation with fixed downstream regressions before introducing an adaptive alternative.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
section: Regression as a downstream accuracy measure
text:
Regression as a downstream accuracy measure
Regression is not another release mechanism in this comparison. It is a fixed evaluation protocol. For every synthesis method, train the same model on that method’s released rows and test it on the same untouched real evaluation partition. Training the model on the original construction rows gives a nonprivate oracle benchmark; it is not a release and it does not have zero error.
Every task uses the same seven public predictors: sex, age range, education group, employment, marital status, minor-children-at-home status, and PUMA area. The linear target replaces the eleven income bands by the public representatives
\[
(0,5,12.5,20,30,42.5,62.5,87.5,125,175,225)
\]
in thousands of dollars. The binary target is \(H=\mathbf1\{\text{income}\geq\$50{,}000\}\). We report held-out MAE for the linear tasks and held-out log loss for the logistic tasks; lower is better.
For each target we freeze two model specifications. The main-effects linear model uses ordinary least squares; the interaction-rich linear model uses ridge 1. The logistic models use \(C=1\). The main-effects design has 25 one-hot predictor columns. The interaction-rich design adds all 254 crosses between distinct predictor pairs, for 279 columns in total. A crossed feature such as education × sex must be related to income through a three-way distribution; the linear-model Gram matrix can combine two crossed features and involve as many as four predictors. Therefore even exact one- and two-way marginals do not determine these fitted regressions.
The standing-column comparison below includes only sources already introduced: the original-data oracle, the exact one-way product, the private one-way release, and the all-pairs release. MWEM is not included until it has been defined.

)









Each standing column is the held-out performance of a model trained on the named table; lower is better. The main-effects and interaction-rich rankings need not agree. Matching pairwise tables directly supports many main effects, but it does not fix the three- and four-variable relationships used by the crossed regressions.
Publishing these benchmark scores is free only because Fulton is public. Evaluating or tuning on a private holdout would require another accounted private access.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements — Self-study notebook
text:
A real exponential-mechanism algorithm: MWEM
Measuring all 28 pairs spreads the budget uniformly, while adding every triple would fragment it further. MWEM (Hardt, Ligett and McSherry, 2012) instead spends the budget adaptively on the marginal cells where its current distribution is most wrong.
Let \(x_{ij}\) be row \(i\)’s category in column \(j\). The public query family is
\[
\mathcal Q=\left\{q_{j,a},q_{jk,ab}:j<k\right\},
\quad q_{j,a}(D)=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbf1\{x_{ij}=a\},
\quad q_{jk,ab}(D)=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbf1\{x_{ij}=a,x_{ik}=b\}.
\]
The family contains one query for every cell of every one-column table and every two-column table: \(\sum_j d_j=36\) one-column cells and \(\sum_{j<k}d_jd_k=529\) two-column cells, for 565 scalar fraction queries in total. It contains no three-way cells and no regression-specific interactions. Instead of refitting a joint from measured tables, MWEM maintains an explicit distribution \(x\) over all \(D=29{,}568\) domain cells and updates it multiplicatively.
Each round \(t\) does three things:

Select. Score every remaining \(q_r\in\mathcal Q\) by how far the current synthetic distribution is from the private table, \(s_r=|q_r(D_{\mathrm{true}})-q_r(x_{t-1})|\), and draw one with the exponential mechanism. Each \(q_r\) is a fraction of rows, so substituting one row moves it by at most \(1/n\): that is the score sensitivity.
Measure. Release that single cell with Gaussian noise at the same \(1/n\) sensitivity.
Update. For every domain cell \(j\), \[x_t(j)\;\propto\;x_{t-1}(j)\,\exp\!\Big(A_r(j)\,\frac{y_r-q_r(x_{t-1})}{2}\Big),\] where \(A_r\in\{0,1\}^D\) is one exactly on the domain cells inside the selected marginal cell.

Only steps 1 and 2 touch the private table. With \(T=100\) rounds and \(\rho/(2T)\) for each, the ledger composes to the same total \(\rho\) as every other release here.
Two implementation details matter. First, a single pass of step 3 moves the weights far too little: selecting all 565 queries with no noise at all only takes the mean workload error from \(0.111\) to \(0.072\). Hardt, Ligett and McSherry therefore re-apply the update over all measurements released so far, several passes per round. That loop re-reads already-released noisy values, so it is postprocessing and costs no budget — but it is what makes the algorithm converge. Second, the reported distribution is the average of the round iterates, as in their Algorithm 1; the final iterate usually scores better, but choosing it on that basis would be tuning the output on the private result.
The other classical exponential-mechanism answer, smallDB, selects an entire small synthetic database from the set of all databases of size \(m\) over the domain. That range has \(\binom{D+m-1}{m}\) elements, so it is a theoretical construction rather than something we can run here.
The next figure checks exactly those 565 cells. For each cell, its error is the absolute difference between the cell fraction in the released table and in the original table. The panels report the average and the largest error separately for the 36 one-column cells and the 529 two-column cells, in percentage points. section: Closing: the workload remains part of the release
text:
Closing: the workload remains part of the release
Private measurements can support useful synthetic tables, but only through the statistics, model family, and public workload chosen before private access. One-ways, all pairs, and MWEM’s adaptive selection pay for different promises; no row generator turns one promise into all of them.
The next lecture changes domains and starts again from a classical low-rank Gaussian construction before asking what a learned generator adds.

Reading map
smallDB privately chooses a small database; MWEM selects a worst query and applies multiplicative weights; PrivBayes assembles low-order conditionals; MST/Private-PGM reconstructs a graphical model; AIM adapts selection and measurement to a workload. These are extensions, not extra headline methods.

title: Private linear regression
text:

    get_ipython().run_line_magic('load_ext', 'autoreload')

try:
    import libdpy
except ImportError:
    %pip install -q "libdpy[notebook] @ git+https://github.com/applied-dp-course/pub_lib.git@main"
    import libdpy
Lectures 5 and 6 built differential privacy for statisticians: private means, quantiles, medians, subgroup gaps, and the local/smooth-sensitivity machinery that made one audited number safe to release. This lecture keeps the audit habit — proposal, diagnosis, repair — but changes what gets released. Instead of a scalar, the release is a model: a weight vector \(\hat w\) that a downstream user will multiply against new feature vectors it has never seen. The question is the same one as always (how much can a single row move the release?), but the answer now depends on geometry — the shape of the feature cloud — in a way a scalar mean never had to.
Running example. We use the Communities and Crime benchmark (sml gate-selection below): each row describes a community, the feature columns are demographic and economic covariates, and the label is a crime-rate statistic. In a fully private pipeline the bounds on \(\|x_i\|_2\) and \(|y_i|\) would themselves have to be privately estimated — exactly the clipping problem Lecture 5 spent three sections repairing. Here those bounds are fixed so this lecture’s attention stays on regression.
Public contract (row-DP): \(\|x_i\|_2\le 1\), \(|y_i|\le 1\), adjacency is fixed-size row replacement, \(\delta=1/n^2\). Nothing about a row is public by default — not the features, not the label. That is the harder element contract, and getting it right is most of this lecture.
Where OLS lives inside the contract. Ordinary least squares solves \(\hat w=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\); ridge solves the stabilized version \(\hat w_\lambda=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\). Both formulas route through exactly two data-dependent objects: \(A=X^\top X\) and \(b=X^\top y\). \(A\) is pure feature geometry — which directions in feature space are backed by many rows and which are nearly empty. \(b\) is the feature–label relationship — the direction the labels actually pull the fit toward. Privacy noise can land on \(A\), on \(b\), or on \(\hat w\) itself, and where it lands turns out to matter more than the total amount of noise. That is the question the rest of this post answers.

title: Private linear regression
text:
Normalization for the public contract
Real rows and responses are mapped into a bounded regime the mechanisms assume: \(\|x_i\|_2\le 1\) and \(|y_i|\le 1\). The implementation uses train-only standardization, row normalization, and target scaling so the public contract is explicit.

title: Private linear regression
text:
Linear regression setting
Empirical squared loss with design matrix \(X\) and targets \(y\):
\[\hat w = \arg\min_w \|Xw-y\|_2^2,\qquad
\hat w=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\quad\text{(OLS)},\qquad
\hat w_\lambda=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\quad\text{(ridge)}.\]

title: Private linear regression
section: Sufficient statistics — covariance, inverse covariance, and leverage
text:
Sufficient statistics — covariance, inverse covariance, and leverage
For squared-loss regression the solver uses \(A=X^\top X\) and \(b=X^\top y\). In the two-feature view, the feature block of \(X^\top X\) is the second-moment geometry of the feature cloud. If the feature cloud is close to Gaussian, this looks like a covariance ellipse.
The inverse \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) is the geometry the solver applies to the right-hand side. A weakly supported direction is thin in \(X^\top X\) but large in \((X^\top X)^{-1}\). A replacement point pointing in that weak direction has high leverage: it can move the fitted plane more than an equally distant point in a well-supported direction. The vector \(X^\top y\) lives in the same coordinates but is a different object — the labels projected onto the features, not a point on the ellipse. The solver combines them as \(\hat w=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\), so replacing a row shifts both pieces independently.

section: Element replacement, now with statistics beside the model
text:
Element replacement, now with statistics beside the model
Drag the red row in feature space and change its height with the slider. The fitted plane updates beside the inverse-Gram ellipse and the \(X^\top y/n\) center, which are the sufficient-statistics objects a direct statistic mechanism must privatize.

title: Private linear regression
section: Analyze Gauss — direct noisy sufficient statistics
text:
Analyze Gauss — direct noisy sufficient statistics
The first repair idea is direct: add Gaussian noise to \(X^\top X\) and \(X^\top y\), then solve from the noisy pair. This uses the same two-feature witness as the preceding sufficient-statistics views. The sampled view keeps the data-plane panel beside the statistic-space panel: noisy draws appear as many inverse-Gram ellipses and many released \(X^\top y/n\) centers.
Algorithm (Analyze Gauss). Input: rows bounded so one replacement changes \(A=X^\top X\) and \(b=X^\top y\) by at most \(\Delta=2\) (spectral / Euclidean norm); budget \((\epsilon,\delta)\).

Compute the clean statistics \(A=X^\top X\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) and \(b=X^\top y\in\mathbb R^d\).
Calibrate a single Gaussian scale \(\sigma=\sigma(\epsilon,\delta,\Delta)\) from the usual Gaussian-mechanism condition \(\delta \ge \Phi\!\big(-\tfrac{\Delta}{2\sigma}+\tfrac{\sigma\epsilon}{\Delta}\big)-e^{\epsilon}\Phi\!\big(-\tfrac{\Delta}{2\sigma}-\tfrac{\sigma\epsilon}{\Delta}\big)\).
Draw a symmetric noise matrix \(N\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) (i.i.d. \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) on and above the diagonal, reflected) and \(\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\).
Release \(\tilde A = A+\sigma N\) and \(\tilde b = b+\sigma\xi\).
Return \(\hat w = \tilde A^{-1}\tilde b\) whenever \(\tilde A\succ 0\).

Privacy: each of \(\tilde A,\tilde b\) is a Gaussian-mechanism output on a sensitivity-\(\Delta\) statistic at \((\epsilon,\delta)\), so releasing the pair is \((2\epsilon,2\delta)\)-DP by basic composition; step 5 is post-processing. The catch is that step 5 is only well-defined when \(\tilde A\) happens to be positive definite — not guaranteed, as the next section shows.

show_fig(make_sufficient_statistics_noise_sample_figure(mechanism="analyze_gauss", epsilon=1.0))

title: Private linear regression
text:
The invertibility problem
A raw noisy Gram matrix is not guaranteed to stay positive definite. If \(\tilde A\) has a non-positive eigenvalue, the inverse is not a stable regression geometry. This is the regression version of denominator fragility.

show_fig(make_sufficient_statistics_invertibility_figure(epsilon=1.0))

title: Private linear regression
text:
Ridge reminder
Ridge solves \((A+\lambda I)w=b\) instead of \(Aw=b\). Geometrically, ridge adds support in every direction before inversion. That is exactly the stabilization role needed after perturbing \(X^\top X\).

Explore ridge versus one frozen Gram perturbation
Start with ridge \(\lambda=0\) and increase the Gram-noise scale until the orange noisy spectrum crosses zero. Then increase ridge until the blue stabilized spectrum is positive again. Read the weakest direction first: ridge shifts every noisy eigenvalue upward by the same \(\lambda\), but it does not reconstruct the clean gray spectrum or erase the perturbation.
This is a conditioning diagnostic around one frozen symmetric noise realization. The controls do not resample a privacy mechanism, calibrate noise from \((\epsilon,\delta)\), or report predictive error. The static conditioning and invertibility figures above remain the evidentiary fallback; the explorer isolates only the algebraic repair that AdaSSP uses next.

RidgeNoiseSpectrumPlot(height=500, width=940).embed()

Loading interactive… (first load downloads a Python runtime)

title: Private linear regression
text:
AdaSSP — stabilize noisy sufficient statistics
AdaSSP perturbs \(A\) and \(b\) directly, estimates how much stabilization is needed, adds ridge mass, then solves. The mechanism remains a post-processing of noisy sufficient statistics.
Algorithm (AdaSSP). Input: \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) with \(\|x_i\|\le 1\), \(y\) with \(|y_i|\le c_{\max}\); budget \((\epsilon,\delta)\); failure probability \(\varrho=\delta/10\); clean \(\lambda_{\min}=\lambda_{\min}(X^\top X)\).

Split the budget three ways and calibrate two analytic-Gaussian scales: \(\sigma_A=\sigma_{\text{an}}(\epsilon/3,\delta/3,\Delta{=}1)\) for \(A\), \(\sigma_b=\sigma_{\text{an}}(\epsilon/3,\delta/3,\Delta{=}c_{\max})\) for \(b\); reserve the last \(\epsilon/3\) for step 2.
Privately debias the spectrum: draw \(\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and set \(\tilde\lambda_{\min}=\max\!\big(0,\ \lambda_{\min}+\sigma_A\xi-\sigma_A\sqrt{2\ln(6/\delta)}\big)\) (a one-sided, high-probability lower bound on \(\lambda_{\min}(A)\)).
Ridge weight: \(\lambda_{\mathrm{ada}}=\max\!\big(0,\ \sqrt{d\ln(2d^2/\varrho)}\;\sigma_A-\tilde\lambda_{\min}\big)\).
Draw a symmetric noise matrix \(N\) and \(\xi'\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\); release \(\tilde A=A+\sigma_A N\), \(\tilde b=b+\sigma_b\xi'\).
Return \(\hat w=(\tilde A+\lambda_{\mathrm{ada}}I)^{-1}\tilde b\).

Privacy: steps 2 and 4 each spend one of the three reserved \((\epsilon/3,\delta/3)\) slices (the eigenvalue estimate and the matrix release are two separate Gaussian-mechanism calls at the same scale \(\sigma_A\)), and step 4’s \(b\)-release spends the third; total \((\epsilon,\delta)\) by composition. Step 5 is post-processing — adding \(\lambda_{\mathrm{ada}}I\) is exactly the ridge fix from the previous slide, sized so \(\tilde A+\lambda_{\mathrm{ada}}I\succ 0\) with high probability.

title: Private linear regression
text:
Gram-sketch repair
The sketching repair samples a Gaussian sketch whose covariance is tied to the Gram geometry, then solves with a noisy right-hand side. The same sufficient-statistics interface remains: a privatized Gram side, a privatized \(X^\top y\), and a stabilized solve.
Provenance caveat: the Gram-sketch repair used here is a local teaching implementation of a one-step Hessian-mixing idea. Fixed-seed tests guard the current wiring, but this lecture does not claim a fully audited upstream port.
Algorithm (one-step Hessian mixing / Gram sketch). Input: \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) with \(\|x_i\|\le 1\), \(y\) with \(|y_i|\le c_{\max}\); budget \((\epsilon,\delta)\); failure probability \(\varrho=\delta/10\); clean \(\lambda_{\min}=\lambda_{\min}(X^\top X)\); constant \(c=2.5\).

Sketch size \(k=\max\!\big(\lceil c\,d\rceil,\ \lceil c\ln(2/\varrho)\rceil\big)\); tail constant \(\tau=\sqrt{2\ln\big(\max(4/\delta,4/\varrho)\big)}\).
Solve for the smallest per-row mixing scale \(\gamma\) such that \(k\) independent, \(\gamma\)-noised row projections compose (via an RDP-to-DP conversion) to \((\epsilon/2,\ 3\delta/4)\)-DP; set \(\sigma_{\mathrm{row}}=\gamma/\sqrt k\).
Privately debias the spectrum: \(\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(\tilde\lambda=\max\!\big(0,\ \lambda_{\min}-\sigma_{\mathrm{row}}(\tau-\xi)\big)\); residual noise floor \(\gamma_0=\sqrt{\max(0,\ \gamma-\tilde\lambda)}\).
Draw a sketch \(S\in\mathbb R^{k\times n}\), \(S_{ij}\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) i.i.d., and row noise \(E\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}\); form \(\hat X=SX+\gamma_0E\) and release the sketched Gram \(\hat H=\hat X^\top\hat X/k\).
Release \(\tilde b=X^\top y+\sigma_{X^\top y}\xi'\) with \(\sigma_{X^\top y}=\sigma_{\text{an}}(\epsilon/2,\delta/4,c_{\max})\).
Ridge weight \(\lambda_{\mathrm{ridge}}=\max\!\big(0,\ \sqrt{d\ln(2d^2/\varrho)}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{row}}-\tilde\lambda\big)\); return \(\hat w=(\hat H+\lambda_{\mathrm{ridge}}I)^{-1}\tilde b\).

Privacy: the sketch (steps 1–4) and the label statistic (step 5) each spend half the budget, \(\epsilon/2+\epsilon/2=\epsilon\); each of the \(k\) sketch rows mixes every record with an independent Gaussian coefficient, so one record’s departure changes one \(\gamma\)-noised linear combination, giving the same per-row DP guarantee \(k\) times over (composed via RDP). Step 6 is post-processing and plays AdaSSP’s stabilizing role again.

title: Privacy Auditing — Self-study notebook
section: Recap: DP as a bound on the ROC
text:
Recap: DP as a bound on the ROC
Let \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\) be output distributions on neighboring datasets, and let \(S\) be the event “the adversary guesses \(D\)” (positive).
\[\mathrm{TPR}=P(S),\qquad \mathrm{FPR}=Q(S).\]
For this lecture we keep one ROC direction fixed:
\[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{FPR}+\delta.\]
Drag \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) to see the forbidden region the DP guarantee carves out of the ROC plane.
How to read the explorer: the horizontal coordinate is false-positive probability under \(D'\), the vertical coordinate is true-positive probability under \(D\), and points above the DP line are incompatible with the displayed one-sided guarantee. Increasing \(\varepsilon\) relaxes the slope; increasing \(\delta\) raises the intercept. This is definition geometry, not sampled evidence.


Code
PrivacyPlot(
    sensitivity=1,
    std=1.5,
    distribution_types=[stats.norm, stats.laplace],
    epsilon=1.2,
    delta=0.05,
).embed()


Loading interactive… (first load downloads a Python runtime)

title: Privacy Auditing — Self-study notebook
section: Exact inversion for known ROCs (recall, not auditing)
text:
Exact inversion for known ROCs (recall, not auditing)
For a fixed \(\delta\), any ROC point \((x,y)=(\mathrm{FPR},\mathrm{TPR})\) gives the one-sided requirement
\[\varepsilon \ge \log\left(\frac{y-\delta}{x}\right)\]
when \(x>0\) and \(y>\delta\). Known ROC + fixed \(\delta\) \(\rightarrow\) tightest DP line \(\rightarrow\) exact \(\varepsilon\).
This is still exact privacy-profile geometry, not empirical auditing.
The inversion is one-sided because the lecture fixes an orientation for the event and neighboring pair. A complete DP statement also applies after swapping the databases. Here the purpose is narrower: establish the map from one ROC point to a required privacy budget before sampling error is introduced.

Laplace: exact ROC
For Laplace noise, the output distributions are shifts of the same known density. We can compute the ROC exactly and find the smallest \(\varepsilon\) line for a chosen \(\delta\).
Move the controls and look for the line that just supports the ROC: that contact point is the governing event. Because the density and shift are known, there are no finite-sample confidence intervals here. This exact case is the reference against which the later empirical estimate will be judged.


Code
TheoryROCVisualizer(
    distribution="Laplace",
    scale=1.0,
    delta=1e-15,
    selectable_distribution=False,
).embed()


Loading interactive… (first load downloads a Python runtime)




Gaussian: approximate DP
Gaussian noise illustrates how changing \(\delta\) changes the tight line. Drag the \(\delta\) slider to compare.
Unlike pure-DP Laplace, the Gaussian tradeoff uses a nonzero failure probability. Watch the supporting line move as \(\delta\) changes while the underlying ROC stays fixed. The visualization still assumes the distribution is analytically known; it does not estimate a guarantee from mechanism runs.


Code
TheoryROCVisualizer(
    distribution="Gaussian",
    scale=1.0,
    delta=0.01,
    selectable_distribution=False,
).embed()


Loading interactive… (first load downloads a Python runtime)




Logistic: adding another analytic distribution
The same ROC machinery is not tied to Laplace or Gaussian noise. If we can compute the PDF/CDF, we can add another distribution and repeat the exact construction.
\[f(x)=\frac{e^{-(x-\mu)/s}}{s(1+e^{-(x-\mu)/s})^2},\qquad F(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-(x-\mu)/s}}.\]
The question is not whether logistic noise is preferable, but which information makes exact inversion possible. Here the closed-form CDF supplies threshold probabilities for every event. In the next mechanism we keep easy sampling but deliberately remove that analytic access, forcing the auditor to reconstruct the ROC from observations.


Code
TheoryROCVisualizer(
    distribution="Logistic",
    scale=1.0,
    delta=1e-15,
    selectable_distribution=False,
).embed()

title: Privacy Auditing — Self-study notebook
section: From exact ROC to empirical ROC
text:
From exact ROC to empirical ROC
Now define the noise procedurally:
\[Z = Z_1 + Z_2,\qquad Z_1 \sim \mathrm{Logistic}(0,s_1),\quad Z_2 \sim \mathrm{Logistic}(0,s_2),\]
with \(Z_1,Z_2\) independent. The mechanism releases \(M(D)=q(D)+Z\), giving
\[H_0: X=0+Z,\qquad H_1: X=1+Z.\]
Sampling is trivial. But we will not use a closed-form PDF, CDF, or ROC. From here on, the auditor treats the mechanism as a black-box sampler.
The explorer below uses the same empirical ROC widget as before, now on the sum-of-two-logistics mechanism. Press Generate Samples to redraw. Check Compute ε to highlight the governing point and the tight \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) line.
Question for the explorer: which threshold best separates the two sampled output clouds? The staircase is an empirical object: regenerate the samples and both its corners and maximizing threshold can move. The displayed plug-in \(\varepsilon\) treats those empirical coordinates as truth, so it is useful for proposing an event but is not yet a confidence-valid lower bound.


Code
EmpiricalEpsilonFromDeltaVisualizer(
    n_samples=500,
    distribution="Sum of logistic distributions",
    scale=1.0,
    delta=0.01,
    random_seed=4,
    selectable_distribution=False,
).embed()


Loading interactive… (first load downloads a Python runtime)



Threshold handoff for the rest of the lecture
The audit figures below need a fixed threshold \(\tau_\star\) selected from the seeded empirical ROC above. We read it off programmatically so every later cell uses exactly the same value.
The printed threshold, ROC coordinate, and plug-in value form the handoff contract. Reusing the seed makes the narrative reproducible. For valid inference on new runs, selection data and audit data must be separated—or the adaptivity of threshold selection must be included in the correction.


Code
print(f"tau_star = {tau_star:.6f}")
print(f"governing point (FPR, TPR) = {governing_point}")
print(f"plug-in epsilon from empirical ROC = {eps_plug_roc:.4f}")

title: Privacy Auditing — Self-study notebook
section: From empirical ROC to one audit event
text:
From empirical ROC to one audit event
The empirical ROC step selected a threshold \(\tau_\star\). We now freeze that threshold and audit the single event it defines.
\[S_{\tau_\star}=\{x:x>\tau_\star\},\qquad \mathrm{TPR}=P(X>\tau_\star\mid H_1),\qquad \mathrm{FPR}=P(X>\tau_\star\mid H_0).\]
Freezing the event turns ROC estimation into two binomial problems. Under \(H_0\), crossing the threshold is a false positive; under \(H_1\), it is a true positive. This reduction is what lets us replace a visually chosen curve point with explicit counts and one-sided confidence bounds.

Fixed-threshold audit unfolding (same sample as empirical ROC)
The threshold \(\tau_\star\) is frozen from the empirical ROC above. The animation replays the same finite sample, with experiments arriving in a balanced random order shuffled by the same seed. The final audit point matches the governing point from the empirical ROC step. The animation plays once and stops on that point.
Read the running point as cumulative FP and TP rates, not as a sequence of new mechanisms. Its exact final agreement with the empirical ROC is a bookkeeping check: both views use identical observations. Because the same observations selected and evaluated the threshold, this replay is pedagogical and does not solve selection bias.




Same threshold, fresh audit sample (audit seed 42)
The threshold is unchanged, but we redraw a new finite sample. Therefore the final counts and plug-in \(\varepsilon\) can change.
Compare the path and endpoint with the previous animation. A different endpoint is expected sampling variation, not a change in the underlying privacy of the mechanism. This fresh sample is the right data source for evaluating the already-fixed event; the next step translates its endpoint into a confusion matrix.

title: Privacy Auditing — Self-study notebook
text:
Confusion matrix audit
Run \(n_0\) samples from \(H_0\) and \(n_1\) samples from \(H_1\) using the fixed threshold \(\tau_\star\) selected above.
The printed counts obey \(\widehat{\mathrm{FPR}}=\mathrm{FP}/n_0\) and \(\widehat{\mathrm{TPR}}=\mathrm{TP}/n_1\). Substituting those coordinates into the ROC inversion produces the plug-in estimate. Check the counts first: a dramatic estimate driven by one or zero tail observations should immediately trigger concern about finite-sample uncertainty.


Code
audit = audit_point(samples_neg_roc, samples_pos_roc, tau_star, delta_default)
print(
    f"FP={audit.fp}, TN={audit.tn}, TP={audit.tp}, FN={audit.fn}\n"
    f"plug-in FPR={audit.fpr_hat:.4f}, TPR={audit.tpr_hat:.4f}, "
    f"eps_plug={audit.eps_plug:.4f}"
)


FP=17, TN=483, TP=52, FN=448
plug-in FPR=0.0340, TPR=0.1040, eps_plug=1.0169

title: Privacy Auditing — Self-study notebook
text:
A single run is random
The mechanism did not change. The threshold did not change. Only the finite audit sample changed — so the plug-in \(\varepsilon\) is a random variable.
The five values below are a variability demonstration, not a confidence procedure. Their spread shows why reporting the largest observed plug-in value would be anti-conservative. A defensible lower bound must control how far estimated TPR can exceed truth and how far estimated FPR can fall below truth.


Code
rng_repeated = np.random.default_rng(456)
print("Five independent plug-in audits at the same fixed threshold:")
for i in range(5):
    neg = two_logistic_sampler(0.0, n_audit, rng_repeated)
    pos = two_logistic_sampler(1.0, n_audit, rng_repeated)
    run = audit_point(neg, pos, tau_star, delta_default)
    print(f"  run {i + 1}: eps_plug = {run.eps_plug:.4f}")

title: Privacy Auditing — Self-study notebook
text:
Tail bounds and safe coordinates
For fixed \(\tau_\star\), the counts are binomial. To lower-bound \(\varepsilon\) we use a lower confidence bound on TPR and an upper confidence bound on FPR, splitting the total failure probability \(\alpha\) across both coordinates.
\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{audit}} = \log\left(\frac{\max\{\mathrm{TPR}_L-\delta,0\}}{\mathrm{FPR}_U}\right).\]
The code uses exact one-sided Clopper–Pearson intervals on each coordinate.
The confidence rectangle moves in the conservative direction for the privacy-loss inversion: TPR moves down and FPR moves up. Splitting \(\alpha\) across the two coordinates gives simultaneous coverage by a union bound, including boundary cases with zero counts. The price is deliberate conservatism; the payoff is a stated failure probability.


Code
audit_safe = audit_point(
    samples_neg_roc,
    samples_pos_roc,
    tau_star,
    delta_default,
    alpha_total=alpha_total_default,
)
print(
    f"safe FPR_U={audit_safe.fpr_u:.4f}, TPR_L={audit_safe.tpr_l:.4f}, "
    f"eps_audit={audit_safe.eps_audit:.4f}"
)


safe FPR_U=0.0539, TPR_L=0.0787, eps_audit=0.2423




Code
figure = make_confidence_rectangle_figure(audit_safe)
plt.show()

title: Privacy Auditing — Self-study notebook
text:
Naive versus safe \(\varepsilon\)
The plug-in estimate is random and overshoots often. The safe estimate is intentionally conservative.
The explorer uses Gaussian outputs with a known analytic true \(\varepsilon\). The title reports overshoots (runs where the estimate exceeds truth). Plug-in overshoots should be near 50%; safe overshoots should stay at or below the allowed failure rate \(\alpha\) (often much lower because the bound is conservative).
Read the vertical truth marker before comparing the two histograms. The experiment validates calibration in a controlled case where truth is available; it does not prove the correction for every implementation. Finite repetitions can also place the observed safe overshoot rate above or below \(\alpha\), so interpret the rate together with the number of repeats.


Code
NaiveSafeEpsilonHistogram(
    alpha_total=0.05,
    delta=0.01,
    n_audit=500,
    n_repeats=500,
    seed=457,
).embed()

title: Privacy Auditing — Self-study notebook
text:
Extra complications

Threshold selection: \(\tau_\star\) was selected from a seeded empirical ROC so the first audit animation matches the governing point above. The second animation redraws a fresh sample at the same fixed threshold to show sampling variability. With a new empirical ROC sample, the plug-in-optimal threshold may change. The simple confidence correction is valid for a threshold fixed before the audit sample.
Multiple neighboring pairs and multiple events/tests all need statistical correction.
Audits are lower bounds: failing to find leakage does not prove privacy.
Implementation bugs: audits are useful because real implementations can violate their claimed theoretical guarantee.
Score design: a weak statistic can miss leakage even with unlimited repetitions; the lower bound is only as strong as the tested adversary.
Compute and stopping: repeatedly extending an audit until it crosses a desired line is optional stopping and needs a sequentially valid procedure.

These complications all move in the same direction: an audit result is evidence attached to an explicit experimental protocol, not an intrinsic privacy parameter recovered from a plot.

title: Privacy Auditing — Self-study notebook
text:
Summary
By the end of this lecture you should be able to state:

DP can be read as an upper bound on the ROC curve of any membership distinguisher.
If the ROC is known exactly, fixing \(\delta\) determines the tight \(\varepsilon\) line.
Auditing begins when the ROC is not known and must be inferred by sampling.
The seeded empirical ROC selects a threshold; replaying that same sample at the fixed test/event reproduces the governing point.
A fresh audit sample at the same threshold gives a plug-in lower bound on \(\varepsilon\), but the plug-in value is random.
A valid audit uses confidence bounds: lower TPR, upper FPR, with the total failure probability allocated across both bounds.
The result is a high-confidence lower bound on privacy loss, not a proof of privacy.

A reusable workflow is: freeze the claim and adjacency; choose neighboring witnesses and a score; use separate data to select an event; collect fresh audit samples; convert counts to conservative ROC coordinates; correct across every pair, event, and stopping rule; then report the strongest lower bound together with its full protocol. A non-separation leaves the claim unresolved.

1. The learner under audit
Each dot is one record described by two public features; the fitted line is the classifier. The colors show the true label, while the line’s side tells us the prediction. A target matters to an auditor only if inserting or removing it shifts a score computed from the trained model.

What intervention produced the private model we will audit? The Poisson step must match the public \(N_{ref},q,T,\sigma\) contract in both neighboring worlds; otherwise we would be comparing different algorithms rather than one target row.
For each update, Poisson-sample rows at \(q\), clip each gradient to \(C\), add \(N(0,(\sigma C)^2I)\) to the sum, and divide by fixed public \(qN_{ref}\). An empty sample still updates with noise.

2. Auditing is a hypothesis test
Train repeatedly with the fixed target absent (\(H_0\)) and present (\(H_1\)), score that target, choose a threshold, and inspect the attack ROC. The two score distributions are empirical because every point comes from a fresh randomized training run; their overlap is the attacker’s uncertainty.
A small audit is just a threshold test. The next cell is the runnable core: change the four toy scores or the threshold and recompute its false- and true-positive rates. The canonical ROC below applies the same operation to every unique threshold in the persisted retraining samples.

section: 3. Label inference is not automatically reconstruction
text:
3. Label inference is not automatically reconstruction
At an approximate logistic optimum, \(X^Ty \approx X^Tp_w(X)\). Does solving that relation recover training labels more readily than held-out labels? Compare the two bars: similar recovery can reflect ordinary feature structure, while a train-only advantage is a diagnostic. Neither is proof of reconstruction or membership.

title: Auditing Machine Learning — Self-study notebook
section: 4. Which score does the attacker threshold?
text:
4. Which score does the attacker threshold?
For binary logistic regression the relation is algebraic: signed margin \(m=(2y-1)w^Tx\), true-label confidence \(p_y=\sigma(m)\), and our attack score \(-\ell=\log p_y\). Each is a strictly increasing function of the previous quantity, so they produce the same ranking and therefore the same ROC, up to ties. We use negative loss from here onward; three plots of the same ordering add no evidence.

title: Auditing Machine Learning — Self-study notebook
section: 5. When does a fixed row become distinguishable?
text:
5. When does a fixed row become distinguishable?
This is a checkpointed neighboring-dataset experiment, not two summaries of one training run. To make the effect visible in a small lecture experiment, we first fix one high-loss real row; its selection rule is explained in Section 7. For each fresh replicate, we construct neighboring datasets with that same row included and excluded, train both models, and save their states at common epoch checkpoints.
The upper panel averages training and held-out loss from the target-in retrainings. The lower panel scores the fixed row under the target-in and target-out models and reports \(\Pr(Y_{in}>Y_{out})\), with half credit for ties: the empirical membership ROC AUC. Thus AUC \(=0.5\) means chance ranking and AUC \(=1\) means every included-world score exceeds every excluded-world score. The 80% pointwise band bootstraps the retrained models. If AUC rises as training fit separates from held-out fit, the row is becoming membership-distinguishable. That is an association for this learner and deliberately hard target—not proof that memorization caused the generalization gap, and not a universal onset time.


Code
make_memorization_onset_figure(artifact)

6a. Aggregate loss gaps across model classes

They have separate fitted models and data splits, so the comparison is about whether the aggregate train/test-loss estimand extends beyond a linear model—not which model has the better absolute loss. The horizontal coordinate is \(\log_{10}\) loss so the long tails stay visible; the annotated mean gaps remain in raw cross-entropy units.

Neither panel is membership evidence for a fixed target; that requires changing the trained model between neighboring target-out and target-in worlds.

6b. Keep two estimands separate
The phrase ‘training points have lower loss’ hides two different experiments. On the left, the model is fixed and the row changes: this is an average overfitting diagnostic and row difficulty is a confounder. On the right, the row is fixed and the trained model changes between target-out and target-in neighboring datasets: this is the sampling experiment needed for membership inference. The combined figure changes exactly one thing at a time and states the question each panel answers.

title: Auditing Machine Learning — Self-study notebook
section: 8. One-run auditing: change the sampling unit
text:
8. One-run auditing: change the sampling unit
A classical audit fixes one target element and estimates its two output distributions by training many independent models: target excluded gives \(H_0\), and target included gives \(H_1\). That is why the earlier empirical ROC has one score for the same target from each retraining. It is statistically clean, but a complete model training run is the expensive unit.
Steinke, Nasr, and Jagielski (2023) reverse those roles. Their one-run auditing protocol is:

Construct \(m\) distinct canaries and draw independent secret bits \(S_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\).
Add canary \(i\) to the training data exactly when \(S_i=1\).
Train the audited mechanism once. This produces one shared parameter vector.
From that one model, compute one membership score \(Y_i\) for every canary. For DP-SGD below, \(Y_i\) is initial loss minus final loss, the paper’s black-box score.
Guess excluded for the lowest scores, guess included for the highest scores, and abstain in the ambiguous middle.

Write \(T_i\in\{-1,0,+1\}\) for excluded, abstain, and included. The audit retains
\[r=\sum_i\mathbf 1\{T_i\ne 0\}\]
guesses, of which
\[v=\sum_i\mathbf 1\{T_i=2S_i-1\}\]
are correct. Under an \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP mechanism, the probability of seeing an unusually large \(v\) is bounded. We invert that correct-guess tail bound, including its approximate-DP correction, to report a 95% lower bound on \(\varepsilon\). Abstention is therefore a power tradeoff, not decoration: guessing only score extremes raises accuracy, while making more guesses supplies more statistical evidence. Move the slider to see that tradeoff in the displayed \(r\), \(v\), accuracy, and \(\varepsilon\) lower bound.

Why show an empirical ROC too?
The left panel ranks all canaries by loss reduction. The outlined extremes are the canaries on which the auditor commits to an excluded or included guess; the faint middle points are abstentions. The right panel then computes one empirical ROC using only those guessed canaries, so it answers a narrow question: among the examples on which we committed, how well does the score order the two membership classes?
That conditional ROC is intentionally descriptive. It discards the ambiguous canaries after looking at their scores, and all retained scores still share one trained model. It therefore looks better than an all-canary ROC and is not an i.i.d. confidence statement. The rigorous privacy claim remains the confidence-corrected bound computed from \((m,r,v)\).

title: Auditing Machine Learning — Self-study notebook
section: 9. Why one run can be loose: three quantifier gaps
text:
9. Why one run can be loose: three quantifier gaps
The one-run theorem makes the lower bound valid; it does not make one run equivalent to the worst case in the DP definition. Keinan, Shenfeld, and Ligett isolate three gaps. Differential privacy protects every element, against every possible output, even when the adversary knows all other rows. A one-run audit usually observes many elements, one realized output, and scores each element through a model affected by the unknown membership of all the others.

Element gap. DP maximizes over the most vulnerable element. A one-run audit needs many canaries to gain power, so its evidence is distributed across a canary population. One exceptionally leaky canary can be diluted by many ordinary ones. Better canary construction and abstention target stronger elements, but they do not prove that the worst element was found.
Output gap. DP also maximizes over the mechanism’s possible outputs. One training run supplies only one output; a rare, high-leakage model may simply not be drawn. More canaries do not repair a missing output tail. Detecting rare bad outputs still requires repeated runs or additional structural knowledge.
Interference gap. The ideal neighboring-dataset adversary knows every row except the target. In one-run auditing, a canary’s score is computed from shared parameters that aggregate the effects of all other secret inclusion bits. Adding canaries creates more guesses, but can make each membership bit harder to isolate. In the DP-SGD case study, placing canaries on disjoint coordinates removes interference but limits the number of guesses; reusing coordinates supplies more guesses until interference dominates.

The paper’s adaptive one-run audit narrows the third gap by revealing earlier membership bits and conditioning later guesses on them while preserving validity. That can strengthen a lower bound; it cannot remove the element or output gap, and a weak one-run result still does not certify privacy.
The visualization below now measures the interference tradeoff in a declared Gaussian-coordinate experiment. Each coordinate releases the number of included canaries assigned to it plus Gaussian noise. Reusing a coordinate increases the total number of guesses. The purple auditor sees only the aggregate; the blue full-knowledge benchmark subtracts all other membership bits, as the DP adversary is allowed to do. Bands summarize 160 independent one-run trials rather than asserting an arbitrary scaling law.

title: Auditing Machine Learning — Self-study notebook
section: Close: what an audit can and cannot say
text:
Close: what an audit can and cannot say
An attack can falsify an implementation and produce \(\widehat\varepsilon_{audit}\), a lower bound at a printed confidence level. It cannot supply the upper guarantee \(\varepsilon_{theory}\), and a failed attack does not certify privacy. The remaining gaps are victim search, one-run looseness, multiplicity, and canary interference.

A disclosed seed makes the realized artifact deterministic; the stated epsilon guarantees describe the randomized mechanisms with fresh secret entropy. These frozen seeded artifacts are reproducibility demos, not confidential-data DP releases. Never reuse or publish mechanism-noise seeds on confidential data. Sampling, display, resampling, and variation seeds used only after a DP release may remain public.
Privacy parameters: the shared private-PCA covariance release, established DP-VAE seed, and separate 60,000-row DP-VAE each use \((\varepsilon,\delta)=(2,10^{-5})\). The PCA directions are not public: they are learned from the noisy private second moment. The DP-VAE samples become public only after their first DP release; calling them public at the evolution stage does not erase that cost.
Composition: the two PCA class branches compose in parallel. A staged DP-VAE and Private Evolution mechanism accesses the same target sequentially, so those costs add. All eight released Private Evolution alternatives compose; selecting one after inspection does not erase the other seven costs.

Private PCA and both private VAE releases use the same privacy parameters, but their displayed comparisons are not architecture- or population-controlled. title: Learned generators: DP-SGD and private evolution — Self-study notebook
section: Step 2 — What PCA is, and how it becomes a generator
text:
Step 2 — What PCA is, and how it becomes a generator
Represent each row as a vector \(x_i\in\mathbb R^d\). Ordinary PCA centers the rows at \(c\), diagonalizes their covariance, and retains the \(k\) orthonormal directions \(U_k\) with the largest eigenvalues. The coordinates
\[
z_i=U_k^T(x_i-c)\in\mathbb R^k
\]
are a low-dimensional description. The reconstruction \(c+U_kz_i\) is the closest point to \(x_i\) inside that affine PCA subspace.
PCA itself is a representation, not yet a generative model. A classical synthesis proposal adds one assumption: approximate the coordinate distribution by a Gaussian with mean \(m\) and covariance \(C\). Then generate a new row by
\[
z_{\mathrm{new}}\sim\mathcal N(m,C),\qquad
\widetilde x=c+U_kz_{\mathrm{new}}.
\]
Sampling more \(z_{\mathrm{new}}\) values is cheap. It does not add directions to the PCA subspace or repair a poor Gaussian approximation.

section: Step 3 — Apply the construction to MNIST
text:
Step 3 — Apply the construction to MNIST
Use all eligible private rows for each target digit and keep every image at its native \(28\times28\) resolution, so \(d=784\). There is no pooling, display upsampling, or additional quantization beyond MNIST’s source pixels. For each target digit \(a\in\{0,3\}\), disjoint public-embedding rows fix only a center \(c_a\) and a common declared scale \(s=10\). They do not fix any PCA direction.
Write \(v_i=(x_i-c_a)/s\) and clip it to the unit L2 ball. We first compute the exact private mean and full empirical covariance and sample all 784 covariance directions. We then truncate the same construction to its leading ten eigenvectors. Both rows are deliberately NONPRIVATE: they isolate the Gaussian assumption and rank truncation before privacy noise enters.

Any original-to-synthetic gap here is Gaussian-model error—not truncation or privacy noise. The exact empirical moments access private training rows and therefore make no DP claim.

title: Learned generators: DP-SGD and private evolution — Self-study notebook
section: Step 5 — Truncate to ten PCA directions, then privatize
text:
Step 5 — Truncate to ten PCA directions, then privatize
First retain only the leading ten directions of each exact empirical covariance. This is still nonprivate, but it isolates truncation before noise enters. Next apply the same rank-10 sampling rule to a privately released second moment.
Which private-PCA method do we use? The simplest one for this setting: symmetric Gaussian input perturbation, often called Analyze Gauss. Add noise to the private second-moment matrix and then eigendecompose the noisy matrix. This is the basic construction studied by Dwork et al. (2014) and is closely related to the MOD-SULQ input-perturbation method of Chaudhuri, Sarwate, and Sinha (2013).
There is no public basis: the basis itself is learned from private rows. In fixed public units, public-partition 99th-percentile norms are about 0.89 for zeros and 0.90 for threes. For branch \(a\), clip the full-resolution normalized centered vector \(v_i=(x_i-c_a)/10\) to
\[
\bar v_i=v_i\min\left(1,\frac{1}{\lVert v_i\rVert_2}\right).
\]
With fixed public capacity and denominator \(n_{\mathrm{ref}}=6000\), form
\[
S_a=\frac1{n_{\mathrm{ref}}}
\sum_{i:y_i=a}\bar v_i\bar v_i^T.
\]
View the upper triangle as one vector. Under add/remove adjacency its \(L_2\) sensitivity is at most \(\Delta_2=1/n_{\mathrm{ref}}=1/6000\). Add independent Gaussian noise with
\[
\sigma=\frac{\Delta_2\sqrt{2\log(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}\approx0.000404
\]
to the upper-triangle entries, mirror them, and call the result \(\widetilde S_a\). With fresh secret Gaussian entropy as required above, releasing \(\widetilde S_a\) is \((2,10^{-5})\)-DP. Projecting to the positive-semidefinite cone, taking the top ten eigenvectors, sampling a Gaussian in that subspace, restoring the public scale and center, and clipping pixels are all postprocessing. The PCA basis is learned only from the noisy private matrix.
Why is the two-digit release still \((2,10^{-5})\)? Under add/remove adjacency, one labeled row enters at most one of the disjoint digit branches. The branches therefore compose in parallel, so their privacy costs take a maximum rather than a sum. No class count is released.
The public center is used directly, so there is no separate private-mean query and no hidden split of the privacy budget.

title: Learned generators: DP-SGD and private evolution — Self-study notebook
section: Path A — train a nonlinear generator on private rows
text:
Path A — train a nonlinear generator on private rows

VAE Step 1 — Encode, sample, and decode
We start from the successful Keras convolutional MNIST VAE, also reflected in the TensorFlow convolutional VAE tutorial, rather than inventing a small dense image model. Two stride-two convolutions encode spatial strokes; a mirrored transposed-convolution decoder reconstructs them. Our only architectural adaptation is to concatenate the public one-hot digit at the encoder bridge and decoder input.



Basic variational-autoencoder flow from input through an encoder, a sampled latent space, and a decoder to the output.


Read the diagram from left to right: encode an observed row, sample in latent space, then decode. Diagram by EugenioTL, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; downloaded unchanged from Wikimedia Commons.
The conditional variational autoencoder learns an encoder \(q_\phi(z\mid x,y)\) and decoder \(p_\theta(x\mid z,y)\). The encoder does not output one latent code. It outputs a mean \(m_\phi(x,y)\) and log-variance \(v_\phi(x,y)\), which specify \(q_\phi(z\mid x,y)=\mathcal N(m_\phi,\operatorname{diag}(e^{v_\phi}))\). That distribution is the small bell curve in the center of the diagram.
A literal random draw would interrupt backpropagation. The reparameterization writes the same draw as \(z=m_\phi(x,y)+e^{v_\phi(x,y)/2}\odot\eta\), with \(\eta\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\). Randomness is now isolated in \(\eta\), while the path from the loss to the encoder outputs remains differentiable. The decoder maps that latent draw and the requested digit to 784 Bernoulli pixel probabilities.
For one labeled image, the minimized negative evidence lower bound is
\[
\ell_i(\theta,\phi)=\frac1{784}\left[
-\mathbb E_{z\sim q_\phi}\log p_\theta(x_i\mid z,y_i)
+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\phi(z\mid x_i,y_i)\|p(z))\right].
\]
The two terms do different jobs. The reconstruction term rewards a decoded sample that explains the observed pixels. The KL term pulls each encoded distribution toward the simple prior \(p(z)=\mathcal N(0,I)\). Reconstruction alone could memorize useful codes while leaving holes between them; then a fresh standard-normal draw could land in a hole and decode poorly. KL regularization trades some reconstruction freedom for a latent space that can actually be sampled. That reconstruction–regularization tension is what makes this a variational autoencoder rather than an ordinary autoencoder.
The requested digit \(y\) enters the encoder and decoder directly; it is not encoded through invented separated prior centers. During training, the encoder provides approximate posterior samples for observed images. During synthesis, the encoder and the original image disappear. To obtain one marginal image distribution, draw \(y\sim\operatorname{Uniform}\{0,\ldots,9\}\), draw \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\), decode, and discard \(y\). Thus \(p_\theta(x)=\frac1{10}\sum_y p_\theta(x\mid y)\). This is the marginal of a conditional model—not a label-free training procedure—but the displayed output is one joint distribution over images. The nonlinear spatial decoder can represent stroke families that one PCA ellipsoid cannot.


VAE Step 2 — Nonprivate marginal VAE synthesis
First test the model without privacy noise. This VAE section uses every eligible private-target row across raw, unshifted digits 0–9: 51,000 images after the disjoint public roles are reserved. The artificial shift family belongs only to the later Private Evolution support experiment. One conditional model is trained jointly: shared convolutional filters can learn reusable strokes and curves, while the one-hot label tells both encoder and decoder which digit is requested. No digit gets a separate VAE run.
At inference, independently draw a digit uniformly, draw \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\), decode, and hide the digit. The figure therefore shows ten unlabeled draws from one marginal mixture rather than ten label-conditional rows. No evaluation image is encoded to construct the red samples.
Ordinary training accesses the private target and makes no DP claim. Its job is to establish that a conditional convolutional VAE and this marginal sampling rule can produce all digit modes. Because the private model below uses more rows and a larger architecture, this foil is not a matched clipping/noise control.
Execution note. Training is maintainer-only and is never run by this notebook. The established nonprivate, clipping-only, and 51,000-row private networks have hash-checked weights. Their legacy bundle also contains historical losses, gradient norms, and clipping statistics; these are internal non-DP maintainer diagnostics, not released evidence and not part of the formal \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) release. The new 60,000-row private appendix packages hash-checked inference artifacts but no training trace; its receipt states that the later control run was interrupted. Notebook execution loads inference artifacts only.

vae_mixture_evaluation = build_uniform_mixture_vae_evaluation(vae_mixture)
