VAE Step 3 — DP-SGD reminder
At step \(t\), include each private row independently with public probability \(q\). For every included row, compute the gradient of the complete loss,
\[g_i=\nabla_{\theta,\phi}\ell_i,\]
clip the full per-example gradient to radius \(C\),
\[\bar g_i=g_i\min\left(1,\frac{C}{\lVert g_i\rVert_2}\right),\]
and release only a Gaussian-noised sum,
\[
\widetilde g_t=
\frac{1}{qN_{\mathrm{ref}}}
\left(\sum_{i\in S_t}\bar g_i+
\mathcal N(0,\sigma_g^2C^2I)\right).
\]
Under add/remove adjacency, one row changes the clipped sum by at most \(C\). The normalization uses the public expected batch size \(qN_{\mathrm{ref}}\), not the realized private batch size. The accountant composes all sampled Gaussian steps; sampling, clipping, and noise must agree with that accountant.

The table is the actual frozen training and inference contract. The private run uses true Poisson inclusion with \(q=0.1\), 400 private steps (40 expected inclusions per row), clipping radius \(C=0.5\), Gaussian noise multiplier 4.121, learning rate 0.25, and SGD with momentum 0.9. The public capacity \(N_{\mathrm{ref}}=60{,}000\) gives denominator \(qN_{\mathrm{ref}}=6{,}000\); realized private batch sizes are not used as denominators. These are the same privacy parameters as the two private-PCA branches above. The input populations still differ: PCA fits separate zero and three mechanisms, whereas this conditional VAE trains on all 60,000 digits jointly and is marginalized over a public uniform digit draw at inference.

Before trusting the output, the implementation was audited independently. The vectorized complete-ELBO gradients match literal one-example gradients and a finite-difference witness; the global clipping norm and clipped sum match a reference loop; a one-step update matches the declared Gaussian draw exactly; and the accountant recomputes the recorded epsilon. Poisson sampling, latent noise, and Gaussian gradient noise use independent deterministic streams.
The implementation divides each complete reconstruction-plus-KL loss by 784, then clips its full per-example gradient. The constant normalization does not change the nonprivate optimum, but it makes the clipping scale interpretable. VAE Step 4 — Private marginal VAE synthesis

The private-training path has therefore answered one question and opened another: once its DP output is public, can bounded private selection improve that released synthetic population?

title: Learned generators: DP-SGD and private evolution — Self-study notebook
section: Path B — privately steer a public population
text:
Path B — privately steer a public population
This path retains the established 51,000-row frozen \((2,10^{-5})\) DP-VAE seed used by the original support experiment, rather than silently replacing its candidate population with the new 60,000-row model. After release its 1,000 samples are ordinary public data. For digits 0–3 we split those samples into disjoint candidate and refresh subsets, fix the embedding and variation operators publicly, and ask the private target only:

Which public candidates look most like the private target?

That smaller interface is the core idea of Private Evolution. It moves the new private signal from millions of model-gradient coordinates into one bounded vote per row per round. The seed is free to reuse after release, but the five new voting rounds are not. If exactly one evolution mechanism were predeclared and released, its hybrid would compose to \((3,2\times10^{-5})\). The notebook releases eight such private alternatives, so its aggregate is stated below.


Code
show_figure(private_evolution_diagram_figure(artifact))










One vote has sensitivity one
For each private pair \((x_i,y_i)\), find its nearest public candidate among candidates with label \(y_i\) and increment exactly one histogram bin. Removing one private row removes one unit from one bin, so both the L1 and L2 sensitivities of the histogram are one.
Exact duplicate candidates are coalesced for the nearest-neighbor search. A stable hash of the contributing private embedding then assigns its one vote among the duplicate members, so population order cannot privilege the first clone and the one-vote sensitivity remains unchanged.
The next cell is a deliberately tiny, runnable mechanism path. The fixed noise vector is public teaching arithmetic—not a claimed private draw. Compare neighboring datasets that differ only by the last private point.

In the canonical mechanism, every labeled private row—including its label—is part of the accounted vote. A “public label” assumption is not smuggled into the sensitivity claim.


Five Gaussian rounds, one ledger
At round \(r\), release
\[\widetilde h^{(r)}=h^{(r)}+
\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{PE}}^2I).\]
The PLD accountant calibrates one common \(\sigma_{\mathrm{PE}}\) so all five unit-sensitivity Gaussian histograms compose to \((1,10^{-5})\). This is one evolution-stage ledger. Together with the earlier \((2,10^{-5})\) DP-VAE release on the same target, \((3,2\times10^{-5})\) is the counterfactual bound only if this one mechanism is the sole PE release.
A bin survives the public within-class family-wise false-support rule only after
\[
\tau_{r,c}=\sigma_{\mathrm{PE}}
\Phi^{-1}(1-0.05/B_{r,c}),\qquad
w_j=\max\{\widetilde h_j-\tau_{r,c},0\}.
\]
Normalize the weights and resample within labels. Apply a public one-pixel 2D translation only when it preserves the image’s ink, then refresh 25% of every class from the disjoint half of the released DP-VAE dataset. These operations add no ledger entry. If every weight is zero, the declared fallback is uniform public resampling rather than a private retuning decision.

With independent alternative streams, the canonical artifact selects 5 rounds. The bar is postprocessing of the displayed sweep and is not a ninth PE run. But the same public evaluation set both selects that bar and supplies its reported score, so the result is exploratory and has no held-out utility estimate.


Add the defined Private Evolution release to the diagnostic
Only now, after defining the seed, private vote, fixed-budget sweep, independent composition, and selection rule, add the selected Private Evolution release to the earlier PCA/VAE diagnostic. The fifth bar uses the same digits 0 and 3, synthetic rows per class, public classifier, and TSTR evaluator as the four trained generators. The resulting order is nonprivate PCA, private PCA, nonprivate VAE, private VAE, and the selected Private Evolution release. It reuses the selected sweep output; it is not a sixth private run.

Public support is a separate assumption
The private target contains a public three-mode horizontal-shift family: \(-6\), \(0\), and \(+6\) pixels. Starting from the same released DP-VAE samples, we change only which public shifts are applied to the synthetic seed: Each target row’s mode is assigned by a row-local SHA-256 hash of its own fixed public identity before voting. Deleting any other row cannot change a remaining row’s mode, so this preprocessing preserves the add/remove neighboring relation.

matched: all modes, with counts \((15,15,15)\) per class;
recoverable mismatch: all modes, with counts \((30,10,5)\);
support gap: the \(+6\) mode is absent, with counts \((25,20,0)\).

The first condition is easy, the second asks whether private votes can reweight available support, and the third is a falsification test. The variation operator moves at most one pixel horizontally per round, so five rounds can move at most five horizontal pixels. The absent \(+6\) mode is six pixels from the nearest available mode and remains unreachable with strict slack.

title: Learned generators: DP-SGD and private evolution — Self-study notebook
Learned generators: DP-SGD and private evolution — Self-study notebook
text:
Honest close
Learned generators do not escape the contract-first discipline:

DP-SGD makes the training trajectory private by clipping and noising per-example gradients.
Private Evolution can start from a released DP generator. Its samples are public at the steering stage, but their earlier privacy cost remains in the ledger; new bounded Gaussian votes compose with it.
Public data quality, rare classes, provider/API trust, representation limits, and target-side tuning remain real failure modes.
Evaluation on an additional private holdout would require its own mechanism.
Reconstruction, membership, and attribute-inference attacks remain valuable diagnostics, but a low attack score is not a privacy proof.

The formal ledger is primary. The pictures and scores tell us whether the private release is useful and where its public assumptions break.

title: Learned generators: DP-SGD and private evolution — Self-study notebook
text:
Reading map
Deep Learning with Differential Privacy introduces the sampled, clipped, noised-gradient route used by the DP-VAE mechanism. Private Evolution supplies the select–threshold–resample–vary framework used by the public-steering path. The lecture’s conditional VAE clips each example’s complete ELBO gradient; the DP-VAE term-wise aggregation paper is a useful comparison because it deliberately studies a different aggregation choice.
JAM-PGM uses public information to propose tabular marginal structure. PMW^Pub, GEM, Aug-PE, DP-MERF, and Tabular Private Evolution extend public assistance in other directions. DP-MERF is a useful measurement-to-generator bridge but is not a substitute for this lecture’s DP-SGD generative-model beat.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
text: This self-study notebook derives differential privacy from an attacker’s decision problem. It is meant to be read and run: code is folded, every visual answers a question posed immediately before it, and the closing comparison separates what Laplace, Gaussian, and uniform noise can guarantee. For the code-hidden lecture version, open the presentation deck.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: The contract: one hidden bit, two neighboring worlds
text:
The contract: one hidden bit, two neighboring worlds
We use add/remove adjacency. Fix a target record and two neighboring datasets:
\[
D_0 = D \quad\text{(target absent)}, \qquad
D_1 = D \cup \{z\} \quad\text{(target present)}.
\]
The mechanism \(M\), its parameters, the data domain, and everything common to \(D_0,D_1\) are public. The private fact is the one-bit world label \(b\in\{0,1\}\). The attacker sees one released output \(O\sim M(D_b)\), knows the mechanism and the neighboring pair, and tries to infer \(b\).
The labels \(H_0\) for absent/negative and \(H_1\) for present/positive are conventions. Privacy cannot depend on which world we happen to call positive, so a differential-privacy guarantee must control both directions. This lecture studies one fixed pair to build intuition; the final definition quantifies over every allowed neighboring pair and every decision rule.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: Why choose such a strong attacker?
text:
Why choose such a strong attacker?
Earlier anonymity proposals failed when their threat models guessed too little about auxiliary information. Here we make the pessimistic choice explicit: the attacker may know every public detail and all common records. Only the target’s membership bit remains hidden. This is not a claim that every real attacker is so informed. It is a way to make the promise survive future side information.
Cryptography can hide a message while authorized parties retain a secret key. A useful statistical release has no analogous escape hatch: it must depend on the dataset enough to answer a question. A constant mechanism gives perfect privacy and zero utility. We therefore need to bound how much the useful output changes the attacker’s evidence, rather than demand that it reveal nothing.
Under \(D_0\), outputs follow \(P=M(D_0)\); under \(D_1\), they follow \(Q=M(D_1)\). Membership inference has become a binary hypothesis test based on a single draw.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: Question: what does the attacker actually observe?
text:
Question: what does the attacker actually observe?
Start with a visible proxy for the two output laws:
\[
H_0: O\sim\mathcal N(0,1), \qquad H_1: O\sim\mathcal N(1,1).
\]
Before looking at the figure, predict where an output would be strong evidence for \(H_1\), where it would favor \(H_0\), and where the laws overlap too much for a confident guess. The overlap—not the distance between two means by itself—is the attacker’s uncertainty.


Code
dist_neg = norm(0, 1)
dist_pos = norm(1, 1)
make_hypothesis_distributions_figure(dist_neg, dist_pos);

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: Question: how should one output become a guess?
text:
Question: how should one output become a guess?
A decision rule maps an observed output to \(0\) or \(1\), possibly using randomness. For these equal-variance Gaussians, a natural rule guesses \(H_1\) when \(O>\tau\). Moving \(\tau\) left makes the attacker say “present” more often in both worlds; moving it right makes that guess rarer.
With \(\tau=0.35\), which shaded region is evidence for presence? Which errors grow if the threshold moves left? Answer first, then use the visual to check the geometry.


Code
tau = 0.35
make_threshold_decision_rule_figure(dist_neg, dist_pos, tau);

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
text:
From regions to rates
The two rates we track are
\[
\operatorname{FPR}(\tau)=\Pr_{O\sim H_0}[O>\tau],\qquad
\operatorname{TPR}(\tau)=\Pr_{O\sim H_1}[O>\tau].
\]
They are conditional probabilities, so they do not depend on a population membership prior. That matters: if only one person in a million participated, the strategy “always guess absent” has nearly 100% accuracy without reading the release. Accuracy would call that attack excellent even though it learned nothing. FPR and TPR expose the actual distinguishing behavior.
A deployment may care about one operating point—for example, very low FPR—but a privacy promise cannot assume every future attacker has the same costs. We need the whole tradeoff across rules.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: Question: what happens when the threshold moves?
text:
Question: what happens when the threshold moves?
Every decision rule produces one point \((\mathrm{FPR},\mathrm{TPR})\) in the ROC plane. Randomly guessing “present” with probability \(p\) produces \((p,p)\), the diagonal. Sweeping a threshold produces a curve. A curve that bows far toward the upper-left gives the attacker high detection at low false-alarm cost; a curve near the diagonal offers little advantage.
Predict whether the shifted Gaussians lie above or below the random-guess diagonal, then inspect the analytic curve.


Code
fpr, tpr = threshold_roc_curve(dist_neg, dist_pos)
make_analytic_roc_curve_figure(fpr, tpr);

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: Question: what makes the attack easier?
text:
Question: what makes the attack easier?
Keep the means at 0 and 1 and vary the shared standard deviation. Smaller noise separates the laws relative to their spread; larger noise makes them harder to distinguish. Which curve should be closest to the upper-left corner? Which should approach random guessing?


Code
results = roc_curves_by_std(norm, 0, 1, [0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5])
make_analytic_roc_curves_by_std_figure(results);









The family of curves makes a crucial distinction. Noise changes an operational attack tradeoff, not merely the appearance of two density plots. At \(\sigma=0.2\), many outputs nearly identify the world. At \(\sigma=5\), the same mean shift is small relative to the noise, so the curve approaches the diagonal.
This still examines threshold rules on the observed value. Such a threshold is optimal for equal-variance Gaussians because their likelihood ratio is monotone. It need not be optimal for arbitrary distributions.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
text:
Exercise: two binomial laws
Let \(H_0=\operatorname{Bin}(5,0.5)\) and \(H_1=\operatorname{Bin}(5,0.25)\). The output is one of \(0,1,\ldots,5\).

Compute \(Q(i)/P(i)\) for every output \(i\).
Order outcomes from strongest evidence for \(H_1\) to strongest evidence for \(H_0\).
Add outcomes to the positive region in that order and compute the cumulative FPR and TPR.
Plot those operating points. Because the output is discrete, randomization at a boundary fills the line segments between them.

Notice that an upper threshold on the numeric output is not automatically correct: here smaller counts favor \(H_1\). The likelihood ratio, rather than the raw value, determines the ordering.


Code
make_empty_roc_plane_figure();

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: Question: how does one threshold trace the ROC?
text:
Question: how does one threshold trace the ROC?
For the Gaussian pair, move the threshold from far left to far right. The distribution panel shows the decision region; the ROC panel shows the corresponding operating point. Check the endpoints: always guessing present gives \((1,1)\), while never guessing present gives \((0,0)\).


Code
ROCDecisionVisualizer(
    dist0_family="norm",
    dist0_args=(0.0, 1.0),
    dist1_family="norm",
    dist1_args=(1.0, 1.0),
    by_threshold=True,
).embed()

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: Question: is a threshold always smooth and forgiving?
text:
Question: is a threshold always smooth and forgiving?
Now compare shifted uniform laws. Their supports only partly overlap, so some outputs occur in one world and are impossible in the other. Predict what happens to the ROC when the threshold crosses a non-overlap region. A support mismatch can provide decisive evidence even when most outputs look similar.


Code
ROCDecisionVisualizer(
    dist0_family="uniform",
    dist0_args=(0.0, 3.0),
    dist1_family="uniform",
    dist1_args=(1.0, 3.0),
    by_threshold=True,
).embed()


Loading interactive…

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
text:
The Neyman–Pearson rule
For densities or probability masses \(p(o)\) under \(H_0\) and \(q(o)\) under \(H_1\), the most powerful rule at a fixed false-positive budget selects outcomes with the largest likelihood ratio
\[
\Lambda(o)=\frac{q(o)}{p(o)}
\]
first. Equivalently, threshold the log-likelihood ratio \(L(o)=\log q(o)-\log p(o)\), randomizing at the boundary when necessary. This is the Neyman–Pearson lemma.
A raw-value threshold is only a convenient special case when \(L(o)\) is monotone in \(o\). Likelihood-ratio ordering handles multimodal, discrete, and support-mismatched laws without that assumption.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: Question: what if we choose the false-positive budget first?
text:
Question: what if we choose the false-positive budget first?
Operationally, an auditor may say “allow FPR \(=0.05\); maximize TPR” rather than choose a numeric threshold. The next view controls FPR directly and lets the likelihood-ratio rule recover the corresponding threshold and operating point. Confirm that increasing the allowed FPR cannot make the optimal TPR decrease.


Code
ROCDecisionVisualizer(
    dist0_family="norm",
    dist0_args=(0.0, 1.0),
    dist1_family="norm",
    dist1_args=(1.0, 1.0),
    by_threshold=False,
).embed()


Loading interactive…

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: Back to privacy: translate every object
text:
Back to privacy: translate every object
The statistical and privacy languages now line up exactly:



Privacy object
Hypothesis-testing object




neighboring datasets \(D_0,D_1\)
hypotheses \(H_0,H_1\)


output laws \(M(D_0),M(D_1)\)
distributions \(P,Q\)


membership inference attack
decision rule


accusation event \(S\)
positive decision region


absent person accused
false positive


present person detected
true positive



The guarantee must hold for every neighboring pair and every measurable event \(S\), because the attacker is free to choose any rule after seeing the public mechanism. Bounding a single trained classifier, a single threshold, or an average-case pair is therefore not a differential-privacy guarantee.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: Question: what shape does differential privacy impose?
text:
Question: what shape does differential privacy impose?
If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP, then for every event \(S\)
\[
Q(S)\le e^\varepsilon P(S)+\delta
\quad\text{and}\quad
P(S)\le e^\varepsilon Q(S)+\delta.
\]
For the attack event “guess present,” \(P(S)=\mathrm{FPR}\) and \(Q(S)=\mathrm{TPR}\). The first inequality gives
\[
\mathrm{TPR}\le e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR}+\delta.
\]
Applying the reverse direction to the complementary decision supplies the reflected constraint. Before opening the explorer, predict how increasing \(\varepsilon\) or \(\delta\) enlarges the attacker’s allowed region.


Code
PrivacyPlot(
    sensitivity=1,
    std=1.5,
    distribution_types=[norm],
).embed()


Loading interactive… (first load downloads a Python runtime)

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: The slope and shift are \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\)
text:
The slope and shift are \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\)
Writing the upper line as \(\mathrm{TPR}\le m\,\mathrm{FPR}+n\), differential privacy sets \(m=e^\varepsilon\) and \(n=\delta\). Thus \(\varepsilon=\log m\) controls multiplicative distinguishability, while \(\delta\) permits a small additive exception. When \(\delta=0\), the likelihood ratio must remain bounded in both directions: this is pure DP.
The ROC statement is not a different privacy definition pasted onto DP. It is an operational restatement of the event inequalities, including both neighboring directions. A mechanism is private only if every attack ROC stays inside the bound for every allowed neighbor pair.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
section: Question: what do noise tails and supports imply?
text:
Question: what do noise tails and supports imply?
Hold sensitivity and displayed scale fixed, then compare Gaussian, Laplace, and uniform output laws. Ask three questions before using the explorer:

Is the likelihood ratio bounded everywhere?
Do the shifted laws share support?
If rare outcomes have very large or infinite likelihood ratio, can a nonzero \(\delta\) cover their probability mass?

The plot answers an ROC question; it does not rank mechanisms by utility, because their loss functions and scale calibrations may differ.


Code
PrivacyPlot(
    sensitivity=1,
    std=1.5,
    distribution_types=[norm, laplace, uniform],
).embed()


Loading interactive… (first load downloads a Python runtime)


Laplace noise has exponential tails whose shifted likelihood ratio is bounded when sensitivity is bounded, making it the familiar pure-DP mechanism. Gaussian likelihood ratios grow without bound in the tails, so Gaussian noise cannot provide finite pure DP; it can provide approximate DP when \(\delta>0\) absorbs sufficiently rare tail events.
Uniform noise has bounded support. A shift creates outcomes possible in one neighboring world and impossible in the other, giving perfect evidence on a positive-probability region. Any approximate guarantee must pay at least for that unmatched mass. “Bounded noise” is therefore not the same as “bounded privacy loss.”

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing — Self-study notebook
text:
Summary

Start with a public mechanism and an add/remove neighboring pair; the private fact is one membership bit.
The mechanism induces two output laws, and an attacker is a binary decision rule on one output.
FPR and TPR describe distinguishing power without being distorted by the membership prior.
Sweeping rules yields an ROC curve; nearer the diagonal means less operational evidence.
Neyman–Pearson orders outputs by likelihood ratio, not necessarily by their numeric value.
\((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP bounds every attack ROC in both neighboring directions: \(\varepsilon\) is the log-slope and \(\delta\) the additive shift.
Laplace, Gaussian, and uniform noise differ because their likelihood ratios and supports differ, not simply because one density looks wider.

The next lecture reverses this perspective: instead of starting from a theorem and drawing its ROC bound, privacy auditing samples mechanism outputs, fixes an attack, and derives a statistically valid empirical lower bound on leakage.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Our “true data” in this lecture
Fulton is public, so we can inspect these example rows.

From now on, pretend the fixed discretized construction partition—20,613 rows—is the confidential ground-truth table \(D_{\mathrm{true}}\).


Every synthetic release may depend on \(D_{\mathrm{true}}\) only through the explicitly accounted private measurements.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Public contract

Eight fixed Fulton domains; \(D=29{,}568\).

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
section: The mechanism stated by its authors
text:
The mechanism stated by its authors

Query counts of short combinations of case attributes and release them with differential privacy.
Sample synthetic records from those private aggregate counts.
Post-processing transfers the aggregate release’s privacy guarantee to the synthetic records.

The codebook also warns: these are reported cases, not a random sample for estimating worldwide trafficking prevalence.
Microsoft’s algorithm documentation · CTDC codebook

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Before manufacturing rows
If analysts need a fixed table or workload:

release those DP answers directly.


General-purpose rows add modeling assumptions.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Start with a Gaussian
Assume a known variance and one unknown parameter:
\[
X_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2),
\qquad \sigma^2\ \text{public},\quad \mu\ \text{unknown}.
\]

Fix \(n=2{,}000\), \(\mu=0\), \(\sigma=1\), public bounds \([L,U]=[-6,6]\), and \((\varepsilon,\delta)=(1,10^{-6})\).


Under substitution adjacency, \[
\Delta_2\overline X=\frac{U-L}{n}.
\]

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Fit one private Gaussian mean
The Gaussian mechanism releases
\[
\widetilde\mu
=\Pi_{[L,U]}(\overline X+Z),
\qquad
Z\sim\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{(U-L)^2}{2\rho n^2}\right).
\]

For this model, clipping any of the 2,000 rows has probability below \(4\times10^{-6}\). When clipping is rare, \[
\widetilde\mu\approx
\mathcal N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+s_{\mathrm{DP}}^2\right).
\] The DP estimate behaves like an ordinary mean with a smaller effective sample.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Then release Gaussian rows
Sample \(Y_j^*\sim\mathcal N(\widetilde\mu,\sigma^2)\) and release \(Y_j=\Pi_{[L,U]}(Y_j^*)\).

For \(m=n\) and rare clipping, \[
\overline Y\approx
\mathcal N\!\left(
\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+s_{\mathrm{DP}}^2+\frac{\sigma^2}{n}
\right).
\]


Finite row sampling is randomized postprocessing. It cannot weaken privacy and actually contracts the mechanism slightly; we still report the original Gaussian-mechanism guarantee unless that improvement is certified.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
The same three estimators, twice


Density on the left; empirical CDF on the right. Privacy widens the mean once; sampling released rows widens it again.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Second step: the Binomial model
Let \(S\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\) and \(\widehat p=S/n\), with \(n=2{,}000\) and \(p=0.35\). Now \(\Delta_2\widehat p=1/n\).
\[
\widetilde p
=\Pi_{[0,1]}(\widehat p+Z),
\qquad
Z\sim\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{1}{2\rho n^2}\right).
\]

Then sample \[
T\mid\widetilde p\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\widetilde p),
\qquad \overline Y=T/n.
\]

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
The same visual grammar


The released-row curve nearly overlays an ordinary Binomial experiment with a smaller \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\)—in both the mass/density and CDF views.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Privacy from resampling alone

Gaussian rows: clip to \([-6,6]\), then sample \(m\) rows from \(\mathcal N(\overline X,1)\).
Bernoulli rows: truncate \(\widehat p\) to \([0.1,0.9]\), then sample the complete \(m\)-row Binomial output.
Both whole-output guarantees grow at leading order as \(\sqrt m/n\).


The bounds are model-dependent. Without Bernoulli truncation, a neighboring input can give an output positive probability versus zero probability.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
section: How many rows can resampling release?
text:
How many rows can resampling release?


The vertical line \(m/n=1\) means “release as many rows as the original sample.” Both curves use \(n=2{,}000\) and \(\delta=10^{-6}\).

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Inference warning
Synthetic rows are useful output, but they are not fresh observations from the original population.

Their sampling variation comes after model fitting and privacy noise. Standard errors that treat them as independent new evidence answer the wrong question.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Extend beyond parametric families
The Gaussian and Binomial examples each estimated one unknown parameter.

For Fulton, a complete row can occupy \[
D=2\times6\times4\times2\times2\times2\times7\times11
=29{,}568
\] joint cells: 29,567 free probabilities.


Instead of measuring all cells, privately estimate useful smaller tables, fit one valid joint distribution, and sample complete rows from that fit.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
section: Temptation: make every column look right
text:
Temptation: make every column look right
For column \(j\) and category \(a\), measure its normalized histogram:
\[
q_j(D)_a=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf 1\{x_{ij}=a\}.
\]
Under substitution adjacency, the complete vector has \(\Delta_2 q_j=\sqrt 2/n\).

Across the eight columns there are \[
2+6+4+2+2+2+7+11=36
\] released cells—but only eight composed vector mechanisms.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
The private one-way product

Convert the declared \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) to total \(\rho\) and split it equally: \(\rho_j=\rho/8\).
Release the whole histogram vector with independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma_j=(\sqrt2/n)/\sqrt{2\rho_j}=1/(n\sqrt{\rho_j})\) per cell.
Project each noisy histogram to the probability simplex.
For every synthetic row, sample each column independently.


The resulting joint is \(\widehat p(x_1,\ldots,x_8)=\prod_{j=1}^8\widehat q_j(x_j)\).

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
section: What the one-way release gets right
text:
What the one-way release gets right


Education uses four released cells; person income uses eleven. The lower row gives their signed percentage-point errors its own readable scale.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
section: What one-way marginals do not determine
text:
What one-way marginals do not determine

The left panel is Fulton truth. The right panel is a public mathematical independence illustration—not a private release and not a fit to Fulton.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Follow six interpretable joint cells


Truth → exact one-way product → private one-way product → sampled release separates misspecification, measurement noise, and finite sampling.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Measure complete two-way tables
For columns \(j,k\), release the complete normalized contingency-table vector
\[
q_{jk}(D)_{a,b}
=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbf1\{x_{ij}=a,x_{ik}=b\}.
\]
The whole vector again has \(\Delta_2 q_{jk}=\sqrt2/n\), regardless of its number of cells. With budget \(\rho_{jk}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde q_{jk}&=q_{jk}(D)+Z_{jk},\\
Z_{jk}&\sim\operatorname{Normal}\!\left(
0,\frac{1}{n^2\rho_{jk}}I
\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
All 28 two-way tables
There are \(\binom82=28\) column pairs. Give each complete normalized pair histogram \(\rho/28\), add Gaussian noise at its own declared vector sensitivity \(\sqrt2/n\), retain every \((A_r,y_r,\sigma_r)\), and fit one joint.

The 28 vectors contain 529 coordinates. Privacy composes over 28 vector mechanisms—not over 529 scalar cells.


This preserves much more dependence than the one-way product—but spends budget on every pair whether or not the analyst needs it.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
One of the 28 measured tables

Truth → raw private measurement → truncated and renormalized table.

All 28 tables were measured at \(\rho/28\) before this education × income slice was selected for display.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
section: The downside: induced one-ways get noisier
text:
The downside: induced one-ways get noisier

Pair-cell noise is \(\sqrt{28/8}\approx1.87\) times the direct one-way scale.
Summing 11 income cells makes the education marginal about \(6.20\) times noisier.
Summing 4 education cells makes the income marginal about \(3.74\) times noisier.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Overlapping pairs disagree

Seven independently noised pair tables imply seven different education one-ways—and seven different income one-ways.

The joint fit restores consistency by compromise; it cannot recover all noise-free answers.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Low-order measurements can hide structure
Let \(A,B,C\in\{0,1\}\) and define
\[
p_{\mathrm{even}}(a,b,c)=\tfrac14\mathbf 1\{a\oplus b\oplus c=0\},
\quad
p_{\mathrm{odd}}(a,b,c)=\tfrac14\mathbf 1\{a\oplus b\oplus c=1\}.
\]

Every one- and two-way marginal is identical; the pairwise maximum-entropy fit is uniform over all eight cells.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
The parity construction


Opposite parity tables share every one- and two-way marginal.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Temptation: add every three-way marginal

\(\binom83=56\) three-way vectors.
4,154 three-way cells.
Only \(\rho/56\) per vector under the same total budget.
Four-way relationships would still remain unidentified.


Repeating “measure every order” eventually becomes the 29,568-cell full joint.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
section: Regression is an evaluator—not a release
text:
Regression is an evaluator—not a release
Every row uses the same seven public predictors: sex, age range, education group, employment, marital status, minor-children-at-home status, and PUMA area.

Train each fixed regression on the original construction table or on one method’s released table. Test every fitted model on the same untouched real evaluation partition.


The original-data fit is a nonprivate oracle benchmark, not another mechanism.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Main effects and interactions
Linear target: replace the eleven person-income bands by \[
(0,5,12.5,20,30,42.5,62.5,87.5,125,175,225)
\] thousand dollars.

Binary target: \(H=\mathbf 1\{\text{person income}\geq \$50{,}000\}\).


For each target, compare 25 one-hot main effects with 279 columns containing all 254 crosses between distinct predictor pairs.


A crossed predictor must be related to income through a three-way distribution. Even exact two-way marginals do not determine this regression.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Regression accuracy by release

Only sources already introduced appear here. MWEM enters the comparison only after its query family and mechanism have been defined.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
MWEM’s query family
For row category \(x_{ij}\), MWEM’s public menu is
\[
\mathcal Q=\{q_{j,a},q_{jk,ab}:j<k\},
\quad q_{j,a}(D)=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbf1\{x_{ij}=a\},
\quad q_{jk,ab}(D)=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbf1\{x_{ij}=a,x_{ik}=b\}.
\]

This is exactly 36 one-column cell queries plus 529 two-column cell queries: 565 scalar fractions. It contains no three-way cells and no regression-specific interactions.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
text:
Select, measure, update
For each of 100 rounds, MWEM:

uses the exponential mechanism to select one \(q_r\in\mathcal Q\) with a large current error;
releases that cell fraction with Gaussian noise; and
multiplicatively updates its distribution over all 29,568 domain cells.


Selection and measurement split the same total \(\rho\) budget. Repeated fitting to already released noisy values is postprocessing.

title: Synthetic data from private measurements
section: Accuracy on the declared query family
text:

section: From ROC geometry to empirical lower bounds
text: From ROC geometry to empirical lower bounds

title: Privacy Auditing
text:
Where we are

Last lecture: DP as a hypothesis-testing / ROC constraint.
This lecture: what happens when the ROC is only accessible through samples?
Proofs give upper bounds; audits give lower bounds.

title: Privacy Auditing
text:
Recall: the adversary’s ROC
\[
H_0: M(D'),\qquad H_1: M(D)
\]
\[
\mathrm{FPR}=Q(S),\qquad \mathrm{TPR}=P(S).
\]


                        
                                            Privacy bound explorer with ε and δ controls. — open the live interactive

title: Privacy Auditing
text:
Recall: DP line

\((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP implies \[
\mathrm{TPR} \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{FPR}+\delta.
\]


We keep this one-sided direction throughout the lecture.


ROC points above the line falsify the claimed \(\varepsilon\) at this \(\delta\).

title: Privacy Auditing
text:
Flip side: exact inversion
\[
\varepsilon \ge \log\left(\frac{\mathrm{TPR}-\delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}\right).
\]
If the ROC is known and \(\delta\) is fixed, we can read off the smallest \(\varepsilon\) line that contains it.

This is still exact privacy-profile geometry, not empirical auditing.

text:

In the Laplace case, the tight line corresponds to familiar pure-DP behavior when \(\delta=0\), and to the approximate-DP profile when \(\delta>0\).

Logistic

section: When the mechanism is a sampler
text:
When the mechanism is a sampler
\[
Z=Z_1+Z_2,\qquad Z_i \sim \mathrm{Logistic}(0,s_i).
\]
\[
H_0: X=Z,\qquad H_1: X=1+Z.
\]
Sampling is easy. Exact ROC calculation is no longer part of the lecture. From here on, we behave like auditors.

\qquad

title: Privacy Auditing
text:
Why tail bounds appear
\[
\mathrm{TP}\sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_1,\mathrm{TPR}),
\qquad
\mathrm{FP}\sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_0,\mathrm{FPR}).
\]
We need simultaneous confidence bounds on two binomial proportions, so the total failure probability is split across them.

title: Privacy Auditing
text:
Safe direction
\[
\mathrm{TPR}_{L}\le \mathrm{TPR},
\qquad
\mathrm{FPR}\le \mathrm{FPR}_{U}.
\]
Use \(\alpha/2\) for each one-sided interval when \(\alpha\) is the declared total failure probability.
Then
\[
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{audit}}
=
\log\left(
\frac{\max\{\mathrm{TPR}_{L}-\delta,0\}}
{\mathrm{FPR}_{U}}
\right).
\]
To avoid overstating privacy loss, move the empirical ROC point down and right.

Naive versus safe

The safe lower bound is intentionally conservative. That is the price of making a statistical claim.

title: Privacy Auditing
text:
What the audit proves

It does not prove the mechanism is DP.
It proves a one-sided lower bound for the fixed event: any valid \(\varepsilon\) at this \(\delta\) in this ROC direction must be at least the audited value, with high probability.
It can reveal bugs or overly optimistic claims.

title: Privacy Auditing
text:
Extra complications

Threshold selection and re-selecting the threshold on each empirical ROC sample.
Multiple tests and multiple neighboring pairs.
Dependence between samples.
Computationally stronger distinguishers.

Keep these as caveats only.

title: Privacy Auditing
text:
Summary

DP bounds the ROC curve.
Known ROC + fixed \(\delta\) gives exact \(\varepsilon\).
A sampler gives an empirical ROC.
The seeded empirical ROC selects a threshold; replaying that same sample at the fixed test/event reproduces the governing point.
A fresh audit sample at the same threshold gives a plug-in lower bound on \(\varepsilon\), but the plug-in value is random.
Confidence bounds turn the estimate into a valid audited lower bound.

Fix one high-loss real row. At every epoch checkpoint, fresh neighboring retrains measure two different things: model fit above and that row’s included-versus-excluded score AUC below. AUC \(=0.5\) is chance; the band is pointwise bootstrap uncertainty.

title: Auditing Machine Learning
section: One run: reverse the sampling unit
text:
One run: reverse the sampling unit
Classical audit: one fixed canary, many independently retrained models.
One-run audit: many independently randomized canaries, one trained model.

Draw secret inclusion bits \(S_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)\).
Train once on the fixed data plus canaries with \(S_i=1\).
Score every canary from that one model.
Guess out on the lowest scores, in on the highest, and abstain in the middle.

For DP-SGD we use the black-box score from Steinke, Nasr, and Jagielski (2023): initial loss minus final loss.

title: Auditing Machine Learning
section: Which canaries does the one-run audit guess?
text: Which canaries does the one-run audit guess?

title: Auditing Machine Learning
section: What makes the one-run claim valid?
text:
What makes the one-run claim valid?
If \(T_i\in\{-1,0,+1\}\) denotes out, abstain, and in, record
\[
r=\sum_i\mathbf 1\{T_i\ne0\},\qquad
v=\sum_i\mathbf 1\{T_i=2S_i-1\}.
\]
Under \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP, the correct-guess tail is bounded. Inverting it gives a confidence-corrected lower bound on \(\varepsilon\).

The conditional ROC keeps only guessed canaries. It is a useful ranking diagnostic, but it discards the ambiguous middle and all retained scores share one model.


The rigorous claim comes from \((m,r,v)\) and the correct-guess tail bound—not from attaching an i.i.d. ROC interval to the conditional curve.

title: Auditing Machine Learning
section: How the crafted canary was computed
text:
How the crafted canary was computed
We fit the non-private reference logistic model and optimize the canary image pixels directly. With a candidate image (x), label (y), and per-example gradient (g(x,y)=(y-p_(x))x), the reference-set curvature is
[ H=_j p_j(1-p_j)x_jx_j^. ]
The optimized objective is the damped self-influence proxy
[ s(x,y)=g(x,y)(H+10{-3}I)^{-1}g(x,y). ]
We use projected gradient ascent: pixel values stay in ([0,1]), their public L2 norm is bounded, the bias stays fixed at one, and we optimize both possible labels. This is still a non-private, reference-model objective; clipping and DP-SGD noise can erase its apparent leverage, so its audit is evaluated only on fresh retrainings.

title: Auditing Machine Learning
section: Three gaps between one-run evidence and DP
text: Three gaps between one-run evidence and DP

title: Auditing Machine Learning
section: The quantifiers that one run can miss
text:
The quantifiers that one run can miss
Keinan, Shenfeld, and Ligett separate:

Element gap: DP asks for the worst element; one-run evidence is spread across many canaries.
Output gap: DP asks about every possible output; one run sees one realized model and can miss a rare bad output.
Interference gap: the DP adversary knows all other rows; a one-run canary score mixes the unknown effects of all other canaries through shared parameters.

title: Auditing Machine Learning
text:
The interference tradeoff
Disjoint-coordinate (Dirac) canaries can isolate effects, but the parameter dimension limits how many independent guesses fit.
Reusing coordinates yields more guesses—until interference reduces the accuracy of each guess.
Adaptive one-run auditing reveals earlier bits and conditions later guesses on them while preserving validity. It narrows interference; it does not remove the element or output gaps.
The figure is a measured simulation: 48 Gaussian coordinates, 160 independent one-run trials per setting. The purple auditor sees the aggregate; the blue benchmark subtracts every other membership bit. Bands are 10th–90th percentiles.

title: Auditing Machine Learning
text:
Two epsilons, opposite directions

\(\varepsilon_{theory}\): accountant-derived upper guarantee.


\(\widehat\varepsilon_{audit}\): confidence-corrected empirical lower bound.

title: Auditing Machine Learning
text:
Close
An audit can falsify and lower-bound. It cannot upper-bound the strongest attacker.

Failure to find an attack does not certify privacy.

section: Path A — train a nonlinear generator
text:
Path A — train a nonlinear generator

A single Gaussian cannot share nonlinear stroke families across digit modes.


Could one conditional convolutional VAE?

title: Learned generators: DP-SGD and private evolution
text:
VAE Step 1 — Encode, sample, decode
Two stride-two convolutions encode spatial strokes; a mirrored transposed-convolution decoder reconstructs them. The public digit label enters the encoder bridge and decoder input.
The encoder outputs a mean and log-variance for \(q_\phi(z\mid x,y)\), not one deterministic code. Reparameterize as \(z=m_\phi+e^{v_\phi/2}\odot\eta\) with \(\eta\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\).
\[
\ell_i=\frac1{784}\left[
-\mathbb E\log p_\theta(x_i\mid z,y_i)
+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\phi(z\mid x_i,y_i)\|p(z))\right].
\]

During synthesis the encoder and original image disappear: draw \(y\) uniformly, draw \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\), decode, and hide \(y\).

The width-16/latent-2 foil trained jointly on 51,000 private-target rows. The figure is one unlabeled marginal, not ten conditional rows.

title: Learned generators: DP-SGD and private evolution
text:
VAE Step 3 — DP-SGD
Include each row independently with public probability \(q\), compute the complete per-example ELBO gradient, clip it to radius \(C\), and release only
\[
\widetilde g_t=
\frac{\sum_{i\in S_t}\bar g_i+
\mathcal N(0,\sigma_g^2C^2I)}
{qN_{\mathrm{ref}}}.
\]

Sampling, clipping, noise, normalization, and accounting must describe the same mechanism.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
Today’s contract

Adjacency: add/remove one fixed target record, (D_0=D) and (D_1=D{z}).
Public: the mechanism (M), its parameters, domain, and everything common to the two worlds.
Private: the membership bit (b{0,1}).
Observation: one release (OM(D_b)).
Goal: bound every attack for every neighboring pair, in both directions.

Labels (H_0=) absent and (H_1=) present are conventions, not asymmetric privacy promises.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
Why take the adversary’s perspective?

Informal anonymization promises failed when they guessed too little about auxiliary information.
A useful release must depend on data; a constant mechanism has perfect privacy and no utility.
We therefore bound how much the release improves the strongest decision rule.


What statistical problem does that attacker face?

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
Modeling the adversary
The strongest possible adversary knows the inner workings of the mechanism and considers only two possible datasets: one with the target user, and one without them.

How can we model the attacker’s task in this setting?

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
Modeling the adversary
The strongest possible adversary knows the inner workings of the mechanism and considers only two possible datasets: one with the target user, and one without them.

How can we model the attacker’s task in this setting?

Distinguishing between two distributions based on a single draw from one of them.
In the statistical literature this is referred to as hypothesis testing, and in the CS community - binary classification.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
Hypothesis testing and binary classification
Two distributions
Example: \(\mathbf{H_0}\): \(x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \sigma^2)\) (negative) and \(\mathbf{H_1}\): \(x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma^2)\) (positive).

Where does one output favor (H_1), and where are the worlds hard to distinguish?

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
FP and TP

Locate the false-positive tail under (H_0) and the true-positive tail under (H_1).

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
FPR and TPR

The probability that an element drawn from \(H_1\) is marked positive is the True Positive Rate (TPR).
The probability that an element drawn from \(H_0\) is marked positive is the False Positive Rate (FPR).

For a threshold decision rule: \[FPR := \Pr_{X \sim H_0}(X > \tau), \qquad TPR := \Pr_{X \sim H_1}(X > \tau).\]

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
Why accuracy is not enough
If participation is rare, “always guess absent” can have nearly 100% accuracy without reading the release. FPR and TPR condition on the actual world, so they expose distinguishing power without being distorted by the membership prior.

Privacy must control the whole tradeoff, not one deployment-specific operating point.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
The ROC plane
Naturally, there is a tradeoff between TPR and FPR. This tradeoff is represented by the ROC plane. Any decision rule is a point with coordinates \((FPR, TPR)\).

Where should a random guess lie? Where would a powerful attack lie?

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
The ROC curve
For any FPR there is a maximal achievable TPR; the collection of these points is the ROC curve.

Should shifted Gaussians lie above or below random guessing?

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
The ROC curve
Of course, this curve depends on \(\mu_1 - \mu_0\) and \(\sigma\).

Which shared noise scale makes the two worlds easiest to distinguish?

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
Case study: two Binomials
Consider two Binomial random variables: \(H_0 = \mathrm{Bin}(0.5, 5)\) and \(H_1 = \mathrm{Bin}(0.25, 5)\).

Compute the ratio \(P(i)/Q(i)\) for \(i \in [5]\).
Order outcomes by their likelihood ratio before drawing the curve.
What are all the possible decision rules?
Compute the FPR and TPR for all possible decisions.
Draw the ROC curve.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
Case study: two Binomials

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
Neyman–Pearson lemma
Every optimal decision rule is a threshold on the log probability ratio. If the log probability ratio is monotonic in \(x\), a threshold on the value itself is optimal.

Fix an FPR budget. Which outcomes should the attacker label positive first?



                        
                                            The likelihood-ratio decision rule and its ROC operating point — open the live interactive

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
section: Privacy as a bound on the ROC curve
text:
Privacy as a bound on the ROC curve
We model the privacy threat as the attacker trying to distinguish two hypotheses: \(H_0\) — the user was not in the dataset — and \(H_1\) — the user was in the dataset. The two distributions represent the mechanism’s output distribution given each dataset.
The closer the ROC curve is to the diagonal, the harder it is for the attacker to succeed — so a natural privacy definition upper-bounds this curve. One simple option is a linear bound: \(TPR \le m \cdot FPR + n\), where \(m\) is the slope and \(n\) the shift (plus its reflected part for the top half).
For every attack event (S), DP requires
\[Q(S)\le e^\varepsilon P(S)+\delta\]
and the reverse neighboring direction. Here (P(S)=FPR) and (Q(S)=TPR).

How should larger \(\varepsilon\) or \(\delta\) change the allowed attack region?

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
section: Privacy as a bound on the ROC curve
text:
Privacy as a bound on the ROC curve


                        
                                            Privacy bound explorer with ε and δ controls. — open the live interactive

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
section: Is this a new privacy definition?
text:
Is this a new privacy definition?
Did we just develop a new (and more natural) privacy definition than differential privacy?
Apparently not. The two-sided tradeoff bound has slope \(m=e^\varepsilon\) and shift \(n=\delta\). Thus \(\varepsilon=\ln m\) controls multiplicative distinguishability and \(\delta\) permits a small additive exception.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
section: Is this a new privacy definition?
text:
Is this a new privacy definition?
Let’s use this insight to reason about the privacy of several other noise-addition mechanisms:

Which mechanisms have bounded likelihood ratios, unbounded tails, or mismatched supports?



                        
                                            Privacy bound explorer with ε and δ controls. — open the live interactive

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
section: Tails and supports determine the guarantee
text:
Tails and supports determine the guarantee

Laplace: bounded shifted likelihood ratio under bounded sensitivity → pure DP is possible.
Gaussian: unbounded tail likelihood ratio → finite pure DP is impossible, approximate DP is possible.
Uniform: shifted supports contain impossible-in-the-other-world outputs → some events give decisive evidence.

Bounded noise is not the same as bounded privacy loss.

title: DP as Hypothesis Testing
text:
Summary

Neighboring datasets induce two output laws; membership inference is a binary hypothesis test.
FPR/TPR and the ROC curve describe distinguishing power without a misleading class prior.
Neyman–Pearson orders outputs by likelihood ratio, not necessarily raw value.
Differential privacy bounds every attack ROC for every neighboring pair, in both directions.
\(\varepsilon\) is the log-slope; \(\delta\) is the additive shift.

Next: privacy auditing fixes an attack and estimates a statistically valid empirical lower bound.

title: About
text:
Applied Differential Privacy studies how useful statistical and machine-learning systems can be built from sensitive data while limiting what their outputs reveal about any one person. The course begins with attacks on anonymized data and accurate aggregate releases, using their failures to motivate differential privacy as a rigorous adversarial guarantee. Students then learn to interpret privacy through hypothesis testing, audit randomized algorithms empirically, and design private methods for estimation, subgroup analysis, regression, classification, and iterative learning. A final block develops the principles and limitations of private synthetic data.
The course is taught through concrete problems, visual experiments, and interactive notebooks. Each topic follows a recurring pattern: propose a plausible method, expose its failure on a carefully chosen example or neighboring dataset, and build a valid repair. The emphasis is not only on proving privacy, but also on understanding statistical error, model assumptions, and the practical choices that determine whether a private result remains useful.

title: About
text:
Who this course is for
The course is intended for advanced undergraduate and graduate students in computer science, data science, statistics, and related quantitative fields. Undergraduate probability, basic linear algebra, and working knowledge of Python are required; prior machine-learning experience is helpful but not required.

title: About
Exercises and assignments
text:
The exercises place you in the role of attacker, auditor, or private-algorithm designer. You will reconstruct hidden data, test decision rules, audit randomized mechanisms, and repair statistically useful methods whose first versions are not private. Each published assignment is tied to a lecture and lists its expected time; use the syllabus for its current placement.

Class assignments — in-class, interactive exercises.
Home assignments — take-home assignments. None are published for the current offering yet.

text: The lectures form one cumulative investigation of individual influence and useful learning from sensitive data. title: Lectures and self-study notes
text:
K-anonymity
Week 1
Status: Forthcoming
Begin with modern and historical privacy failures, then examine k-anonymity as a plausible first defense. Composition, homogeneous groups, and auxiliary information show why hiding identity is not the same as hiding sensitive facts—and why the course needs a stronger adversarial definition.

title: Lectures and self-study notes
text:
Reconstruction Attacks
Week 2
Status: Available
See how accurate answers to many aggregate questions become constraints on a hidden database. Brute force, least squares, and linear programming reveal both why reconstruction is possible and why enough defensive noise is unavoidable.

Self-study notes · 
Slides

title: Lectures and self-study notes
text:
DP as Hypothesis Testing
Week 3
Status: Available
Model privacy leakage as the strongest adversary’s attempt to distinguish two neighboring datasets. Likelihood ratios, ROC curves, and decision rules lead to an operational interpretation of epsilon and delta rather than a definition presented without motivation.

Self-study notes · 
Slides
Exercise

title: Lectures and self-study notes
text:
Privacy Auditing
Week 4
Status: Available
Reverse the hypothesis-testing view of differential privacy: use sampled outputs and a fixed distinguishing event to obtain an empirical lower bound on privacy loss. Confidence intervals show why an apparent attack must be corrected for finite-sample uncertainty.

Self-study notes · 
Slides

title: Lectures and self-study notes
text:
Private Estimation
Week 5
Status: Available
Estimate means, medians, quantiles, and histograms while auditing tempting but invalid shortcuts. The central lesson is that useful privacy often comes from changing the utility measure or privatizing data-dependent choices—not simply adding noise to an ordinary estimator.

Self-study notes · 
Slides

title: Lectures and self-study notes
text:
Private Subgroup Comparisons After Clipping
Week 6
Status: Available
Once the value range is controlled, subgroup analysis becomes a problem of denominators and data-dependent stability. Compare global sensitivity, invalid oracle local sensitivity, noisy counts and sums, propose-test-release, and smooth sensitivity, then introduce private selection and thresholding.

Self-study notes · 
Slides

title: Lectures and self-study notes
text:
Private linear regression
Week 7
Status: Available
Move from private scalar statistics to a private model. Regression geometry, leverage, and conditioning explain why input and output perturbation can fail, while noisy sufficient statistics and regularization show where privacy noise can be injected more effectively.

Self-study notes · 
Slides

title: Lectures and self-study notes
text:
MNIST linear-query classifier
Week 8
Status: Available
Build a visual classifier whose weights are themselves a bounded vector-valued query. A model can look overwhelmed by privacy noise while still predicting accurately, motivating effective dimension and the distinction between population-level signal, generalization, and privacy leakage.

Self-study notes ·

Logistic Regression, SGD, and DP-SGD
Week 9
Status: Available
Open the iterative training loop and identify each example’s gradient contribution. Per-example clipping, calibrated Gaussian noise, subsampling, and composition produce DP-SGD; re-auditing the trained model tests whether the repair controls the worst-case influence exposed previously.

title: K-anonymity
text:
The pressure we inherit

A dataset or trained model can reveal more than an intended aggregate.
Removing a direct identifier feels sensible.
The attacker also has outside information.

title: K-anonymity
text:
Today’s contract

Public: the released table and the generalization rule.
Private: whether a particular person, and their diagnosis, appears in the source table.
Threat: link a target’s public attributes to a row in the release.

title: K-anonymity
text:
What would an attacker know?

Age? Neighborhood? Occupation?


These are quasi-identifiers: not names, but identifying in combination.

title: K-anonymity
text:
Four roles for columns



Role
Example
Privacy job




direct identifier
name, patient ID
identifies alone


quasi-identifier
age, ZIP, occupation
links in combination


sensitive attribute
diagnosis
fact we want to protect


analysis attribute
treatment outcome
supports the intended study




The role depends on the attacker’s information—not the data type.

title: K-anonymity
text:
The tempting proposal

Generalize age to a range.
Generalize ZIP to a prefix.
Ensure every quasi-identifier pattern occurs at least \(k\) times.

title: K-anonymity
section: How much detail buys a larger group?
text: How much detail buys a larger group?

title: K-anonymity
text:
Read the ladder

Exact values: six visible patterns, each with one row.
Targeted age bands: three patterns, each with two rows.
Full suppression: one pattern with all six rows.


The diagnosis column never changed.

title: K-anonymity
text: Equivalence classes

title: K-anonymity
text:
The definition earns its name
A release is \(k\)-anonymous when every quasi-identifier pattern belongs to at least \(k\) records.
\[E_Q(r)=\{r':r'[Q]=r[Q]\}, \qquad \min_r |E_Q(r)|\ge k.\]

The promise is plausible deniability about which row is yours.

title: K-anonymity
text:
What did we protect?

Direct identity is blurred inside a group.
The sensitive value has not yet entered the definition.
That omission is the next attack surface.

title: K-anonymity
text:
Three boundaries on the promise

It protects only the declared quasi-identifiers \(Q\).
It does not state a membership guarantee.
It constrains class size, not sensitive-value uncertainty.

Diagnosis

Both people are indistinguishable by quasi-identifiers.

title: K-anonymity
text: Proposal → diagnosis → repair

title: K-anonymity
text:
First repair: l-diversity

Ask for several sensitive values inside every class.
This blocks the simplest homogeneous-class attack.
It still depends on what the attacker knows and which releases they can combine.

title: K-anonymity
text:
Second repair: t-closeness

Compare each class’s sensitive-value distribution to the population.
A class can be diverse yet reveal a strikingly unusual distribution.
Stronger tabular definitions buy privacy by reducing utility and interpretability.

title: K-anonymity
text:
The composition question
What if three individually \(2\)-anonymous tables are released?

Each table hides a different column.


Together, their consistency constraints can act like a Sudoku puzzle.

title: K-anonymity
text:
How the Sudoku attack works

Expand each generalized row into possible original rows.
Intersect the candidate sets across releases.
Keep multiplicities required by every release.


Ambiguous clues can have a unique joint solution.

title: K-anonymity
section: No composition rule for class size
text:
No composition rule for class size

Each release creates a different partition of the people.
Intersecting two size-\(k\) classes can create a singleton.
A sensitive value in one release can identify a class in another.

title: K-anonymity
section: Composition is not an edge case
text:
Composition is not an edge case

Attackers see auxiliary data.
They see earlier releases.
They may know the anonymization algorithm.
Small clues combine into a strong inference.

title: K-anonymity
section: The algorithm may be side information
text:
The algorithm may be side information
Suppose the anonymizer always chooses the smallest generalization that reaches \(k\).

The boundary it chose—and the finer boundary it did not choose—becomes evidence about the data.

title: K-anonymity
section: Privacy and utility pull on the same cells
text:
Privacy and utility pull on the same cells

Exact values support fine-grained analysis.
Targeted bands reduce linkage and resolution.
Full suppression maximizes the class and erases the analysis.


\(k\) is a class-size promise, not a utility score.

title: K-anonymity
text:
Why this matters beyond tables

Modern model-extraction and reconstruction attacks also aggregate weak signals.
“No one output reveals everything” is not a guarantee.
A privacy definition must quantify over what an attacker can observe.

title: K-anonymity
text:
Common footing



Question
k-anonymity




Hides direct identity?
Sometimes


Hides a homogeneous sensitive value?
No


Survives multiple releases by construction?
No


Models arbitrary side information?
No

title: K-anonymity
section: What must a stronger definition handle?
text:
What must a stronger definition handle?

A public algorithm.
Arbitrary side information.
Repeated, adaptive releases.
One person’s participation or value.
A quantitative rule for composition.

title: K-anonymity
text:
Bridge
We need a guarantee that compares neighboring datasets and remains meaningful when an attacker knows everything except one person’s participation.

That is the pressure that leads to differential privacy.

title: Logistic Regression, SGD, and DP-SGD
text:
The pressure from Lecture 8
Lecture 8 privatized one fixed linear statistic. Logistic regression learns through an adaptive sequence of gradients.

We will privatize optimization itself.

Poisson inclusion rate \(q\); clip \(C\); noise multiplier \(\sigma\); integer steps \(T\); fixed public capacity \(N_{ref}\).

\[p(y\mid\theta,\phi)=\exp\{(y\theta-b(\theta))/a(\phi)+c(y,\phi)\}\]
\[\eta_i=w^Tx_i+b,\quad \mu_i=E[Y_i\mid x_i],\quad \operatorname{logit}(\mu_i)=\eta_i\]
For Bernoulli data: \(p_i=\sigma(\eta_i)\) and \(\ell_i=-y_i\log p_i-(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\).

title: Logistic Regression, SGD, and DP-SGD
text:
Full-batch GD first
\[L(w)=n^{-1}\sum_i\ell_i(w),\qquad w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_{GD}\nabla L(w_t)\]

title: Logistic Regression, SGD, and DP-SGD
text:
GD and SGD
\[L(w)=n^{-1}\sum_i\ell_i(w),\qquad w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta\nabla L(w_t)\]
\[w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta |B_t|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_t}\nabla\ell_i(w_t)\]
An SGD batch is random, hence its gradient is random. On 2-vs-3 below, GD uses \(\eta=0.06\) and SGD uses batch 64 with \(\eta=0.15\); both make six full passes. GD has one epoch-end update per pass; the SGD curve retains every mini-batch update, positioned by fractional completed epoch.

A gradient is an additive query
With the intercept included in \(\tilde x_i\):
\[g_i(w_t)=(p_i-y_i)\tilde x_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in B_t}g_i(w_t).\]
Conditional on current \(w_t\), the sum is additive over records. Adaptive composition handles later queries chosen from earlier private outputs.

title: Private Estimation
text:
From auditing to mechanisms

Running problem: estimate a typical income from a private sample.
Tempting estimators often work on ordinary data.
Differential privacy is a worst-case neighboring-dataset claim.


Question: How do we turn a failed estimator into a valid mechanism without losing the statistical goal?

title: Private Estimation
text:
Today’s contract

Dataset size: \(n=1{,}000\).
Adjacency: substitute one row.
Total budget per released estimate: $arepsilon=1$ and the course value of \(delta\).
Accuracy target: sample or population mean, except when we deliberately switch to a median.
Data example: Fulton PUMS income.

Every proposal must state its target, public inputs, private computations, and released output.

title: Private Estimation
text:
The loop we will repeat

Propose the estimator we wish were safe.
Audit it on a chosen neighboring pair.
Diagnose the exact data-dependent step.
Repair that step with a mechanism and account for its budget.


Question: Which step protects us from mistaking “stable on my sample” for privacy?

title: Private Estimation
text:
Public-menu contract

Grids, bin edges, candidate thresholds, and transforms are fixed before private data is touched.
Public data may choose the menu.
Private data must privately choose from the menu.

Post-processing protects later computation only after every private choice has already been made by a DP mechanism.

title: Private Estimation
section: Oracle EDA — not a private release
text:
Oracle EDA — not a private release


Question: Which choices in this exact histogram would change if one row changed?

title: Private Estimation
text:
Proposal 1 — bounded-range mean
Assume every value is publicly known to lie in \([L,U]\) and release
\[\bar x+\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}^2),
\qquad \Delta_2(\bar x)=\frac{U-L}{n}.\]
This is a valid template when the range and Gaussian calibration are public.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Sensitivity sets the noise scale

A conservative salary domain can be far wider than the observed data.
Here the public width is \(10^8\) dollars.
At \(n=1{,}000\), the calibrated noise standard deviation is about 187,788 dollars.

The mechanism may be private and still be useless for a mean near tens of thousands of dollars.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Valid—but useful?


Question: Did privacy fail here, or did the public sensitivity bound destroy utility?

title: Private Estimation
text:
Diagnosis 1 — bound first

Adding noise is not the design step; bounding contribution is.
A huge public range makes the raw mean private at huge cost.
A narrow range would help—but learning it from private data is itself a private computation.

The next proposals try to discover a useful clipping range.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Proposal 2 — empirical \(\mu\pm4\sigma\)

Compute the sample mean \(\hat\mu\) and standard deviation \(\hat\sigma\).
Clip each row to \([\hat\mu-4\hat\sigma,\hat\mu+4\hat\sigma]\).
Add noise calibrated to the learned width.


Question: What else changed besides the final clipped mean when one row changed?

title: Private Estimation
section: A typical audit may look fine
text:
A typical audit may look fine

This finite audit does not cross the claimed \(\varepsilon=1\) bound on its chosen pair.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Why the audit is one-sided

Finding a separating witness disproves a privacy claim.
Failing to find one does not quantify over all neighboring datasets and events.
Here both the clipping interval and the output noise scale depend on private data.


Question: Can an empirical audit ever certify the universal DP definition?

title: Private Estimation
section: Diagnosis 2 — preprocessing is part of the release
text:
Diagnosis 2 — preprocessing is part of the release
The mechanism is not
\[\text{fixed clipping}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{DP mean}.\]
It is
\[D\longrightarrow(\hat\mu(D),\hat\sigma(D))
\longrightarrow\text{data-dependent clipping and noise}.\]
Those first arrows need privacy accounting too.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Proposal 3 — empirical quantile clipping

Learn the 1st and 99th percentiles from the private sample.
Clip to those empirical thresholds.
Release a noisy clipped mean.

Quantiles are robust on typical data, but the learned order statistics can jump across a constructed gap.

title: Private Estimation
text:
A witness catches the leak


Question: Why can the output laws separate even though the final mean is clipped?

title: Private Estimation
text:
Diagnosis 3 — post-processing starts too late

The lower and upper thresholds are data-dependent.
They change both the deterministic clipped mean and its noise scale.
Noise on the final number does not privatize thresholds that were learned non-privately.

The repair must privatize the bounds before using them.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Repair 1 — private quantile-clipped mean

Select public threshold candidates with private rank scores, then clip and release the mean.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Composition is a ledger

The total is \(\varepsilon=1\) by sequential composition.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Reallocate without changing the guarantee


        
        
        


                            
                                            


Move the bounds’ share; the slices still sum to \(\varepsilon=1\). The proxy is bookkeeping, not measured error—choose an allocation with an accuracy experiment.

title: Private Estimation
text:
A different target — the median
The median resists an isolated outlier on ordinary samples, so it is tempting to release
\[\operatorname{median}(D)+\text{value noise}.\]
But robustness describes typical contamination; DP sensitivity asks for the largest change over all neighboring datasets.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Robust is not worst-case stable

Question: Can one substituted row move the median across an arbitrarily wide gap in the value domain?

Ordinary data may hide the answer. Construct the neighboring pair that stresses the order statistic.

title: Private Estimation
text:
One row, one median gap

The constructed neighbors move the median from $39,990 to $59,996.
Value noise calibrated to the full public range is valid—but can erase the utility of the median.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Repair 2 — change the error metric

The rank utility
\[u(D,t)=-\left|\#\{x_i\le t\}-\frac n2\right|\]
changes by at most one under substitution, independent of dollar gaps.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Inverse-sensitivity landscape


Question: Why is spending privacy on rank error more useful than adding noise in dollars?

title: Private Estimation
text:
From clipping to localization
For a roughly Gaussian population, useful clipping needs private estimates of both scale and location.

Estimating \(\sigma\) from raw values is entangled with unknown \(\mu\).
Estimating \(\mu\) needs a grid whose resolution matches the unknown scale.
Each private choice must appear in the budget ledger.

title: Private Estimation
text:
Localize scale without the mean

Disjoint pairwise differences \(|X_i-X_j|\) cancel the mean; a noisy histogram privately selects a scale bin.

Localize the center on a public grid

The private scale determines a useful public-grid resolution; noisy counts then localize the center before the final clipped mean.

Model assumptions still matter


Question: If privacy accounting is valid but the Gaussian model is wrong, what failed?

title: Private Estimation
text:
Takeaways and bridge

State the target, public menu, private choices, and released output.
Use audits to find counterexamples—not to certify privacy.
Diagnose the data-dependent step before choosing its repair.
Account for every private selection by composition.
Validate statistical assumptions separately from privacy.

Next: use private selection mechanisms to choose which query or model to release.
